script.title: Entry routine & seating
script.do: Students enter, find assigned seat, place backpacks, phones in the back. Greet them by name.
options: Have a name tent at each seat before they arrive.
Use a seating chart on the board; students self-assign to see name order.
script.say: Welcome to chemistry! Before we begin, make sure your phone is put away and you have your seat. You're going to love this class.

script.title: Bell ringer & classroom community
script.do: Project a simple question on the board: 'What is one thing you already know is made of atoms?' (e.g., water, your phone, the desk). Students write on an index card and pass forward.
options: Read a few aloud (anonymously) to celebrate prior knowledge and set a supportive tone.
Keep cards to use as a getting-to-know-you reference throughout the week.
script.say: There are no wrong answers here. Just jot down what comes to mind.

script.title: Meet the teacher & classroom culture
script.do: Spend 2–3 minutes on a personal story: 'I fell in love with chemistry because…' (genuine, brief—maybe how it connects to solving a real problem or something from your life). Show a photo if you have one.
options: Share a quick demo (e.g., baking soda + vinegar fizz) to model curiosity.
Ask one student to share why THEY chose this class or are curious about science.
script.say: Chemistry is about asking 'why' and discovering answers through careful observation and testing. That's what we'll do together.

script.title: Classroom norms & routines
script.do: Co-create 3–4 core class agreements: respect, safety, participation, integrity (keep it short and student-input focused). Write them on the board or a poster and leave them up all semester.
options: Use a rapid fist-to-five poll to see if everyone agrees.
Have students sign a class pledge poster on the way out (optional ritual).
script.say: In this lab, we take care of each other and our space. What's one thing you need from classmates to learn best?

script.title: Bell-ringer & entry routine (teach the habit)
script.do: Teach the daily rhythm: 'Every day you walk in, you'll see a question or prompt on the board or screen. You sit down and answer it—3–5 minutes. Then we review it together.' Do a live model: show the bell ringer card/slide format.
options: Have a bell-ringer template visible (projected or on a handout so they see the format).
Explain: 'This warms up your brain, checks what you remember, and starts our thinking.'
script.say: Tomorrow, there will be a question waiting for you when you arrive. It's your 'warm-up.' We'll talk about it after attendance.

script.title: Video: What is Chemistry?
script.do: Play the short video. Have students note one or two key ideas on a provided handout or their notebook.
options: Pause halfway and ask a quick think-pair-share: 'Why do you think chemistry matters?'
Play without pause, then debrief with the two questions below.
script.say: As you watch, listen for real-world examples of chemistry in action.

script.title: Video debrief & connect to scope
script.do: Ask the two video questions aloud; take 2–3 answers. Affirm each one and tie it to 'Scope of Chemistry'—the idea that chemistry is everywhere.
options: Show a quick 1-minute list of chemistry fields on the board (medicine, agriculture, materials, environment).
Ask: 'Which of those fields might you be interested in exploring this year?'
script.say: You just heard real chemistry. That's what we're diving into. Chemistry is the study of matter, energy, and how substances change.

script.title: Introduce the worksheet & expectations
script.do: Hand out the 'Chemistry and You' worksheet. Walk through the instructions out loud (no more than 1 min). Emphasize: 'This is a low-pressure first day—no grade today. Just your thinking.'
options: Do the first item together as a class (the matching example).
Have them start in pairs so they feel supported on day one.
script.say: You'll match terms, answer 'Why does this matter?' and reflect. This is about building your understanding, not a test.

script.title: Worksheet time & circulation
script.do: Students work individually or in pairs on the worksheet. Circulate, check in, affirm effort, offer a hint if stuck.
options: If time is tight, assign problems 1–4 today, 5–7 for next class.
Fast finishers: 'Move to the Challenge box below.'
script.say: Don't worry about getting every answer perfect. Show your thinking. I'm here if you get stuck.

script.title: Exit ticket & wrap
script.do: Ask students to write on a sticky note (or index card) one answer to the exit question: 'What is one place you see chemistry happening this week?' Collect as they leave (valuable for building community and checking understanding).
options: Read a few aloud at the start of day 2 to celebrate and re-anchor the idea.
Use responses to plan a personal connection story for the next lesson.
script.say: On your way out, stick your answer on the board. Tomorrow I'll read some and we'll see all the chemistry around you.

Mon.notes:
## Key Idea: Chemistry Everywhere

Chemistry is the study of **matter** (anything that takes up space and has mass) and **energy** (the ability to make things change). From the water you drink to the phone in your hand, chemistry explains how the world works.

## Key Terms

**Matter:** anything with mass and volume—solids, liquids, gases, and everything in between.

**Energy:** what makes change happen—heat, light, motion, and chemical reactions all involve energy.

**Scope of chemistry:** the huge range of topics chemistry covers—medicine, agriculture, materials, the environment, and countless more.

## Why Chemistry Matters

Chemistry helps us:
- Develop medicines and vaccines
- Create stronger, lighter materials
- Grow food sustainably
- Clean up pollution
- Power cars, phones, and homes

Think about your day: water at breakfast (chemistry), sun protection (chemistry), battery in your phone (chemistry). It's *everywhere*.

## You Try

**Think of one object in your room right now. What is it made of? What chemical change might happen to it (rust, burn, break down)?**

*Example: A wooden pencil is made of wood and graphite. Over time, wood can rot (a chemical change).*

slides.heading: Welcome to Chemistry!
bullets: Chemistry is everywhere: your body, your phone, the air you breathe.
From medicine to pollution cleanup to the food you eat—chemistry is at work.
This year, you'll learn *why* things change and *how* to use that knowledge to solve real problems.

slides.heading: What is Chemistry?
bullets: **Chemistry** = the study of matter (stuff that has mass and volume) and energy (the power to make change).
**Matter** is everything: gases, liquids, solids, atoms, molecules.
**Energy** makes things happen: heat, light, reactions, motion.
Chemistry explains *how* and *why* matter transforms.

slides.heading: Four Pillars of Chemistry
bullets: **Matter:** atoms, elements, molecules—the building blocks.
**Energy:** heat, light, forces that drive change.
**Change:** physical (ice melts) and chemical (wood burns).
**Applications:** medicine, agriculture, environment, materials.

slides.heading: Worked Example: Why Medicine Matters
bullets: **The problem:** A patient has a bacterial infection.
**Chemistry step 1:** Chemists study the structure of bacterial cells at the atomic level.
**Chemistry step 2:** They design a molecule (antibiotic) that destroys bacteria but not human cells.
**Chemistry step 3:** They test it for safety and effectiveness.
**Result:** A lifesaving medicine—all because of chemistry.

slides.heading: You Try: Chemistry Around You
slides.youTry: Name one object in your classroom right now. What do you think is happening at the atomic level when it dissolves in water, burns, or changes color? (Hint: that's chemistry!)
bullets: No wrong answers on day one—just notice that change is happening everywhere.
Many of those changes are *chemical reactions*—the main topic of this course.

slides.heading: Your Semester at a Glance
bullets: **Next:** Matter, measurements, and how we organize chemistry (Chapters 1–3).
**Then:** Atoms, the periodic table, and chemical bonds (Chapters 4–9).
**Later:** Reactions, energy, equilibrium, and real applications (Chapters 10–26).
**Every day:** a bell ringer, guided notes, practice, and an exit check.

procedureExamples.prompt: Why is understanding matter and energy important for designing a biodegradable plastic?
steps: Step 1: Identify what matters—pollutants are chemical substances with specific properties.
Step 2: Choose a **method** based on chemistry: a filter (physical separation) or a chemical reaction (breaking down toxins).
Step 3: Use **energy** (heat, UV light, or electrical current) to power the process.
Step 4: Test the result to ensure it's safe to drink.
procedureExamples.answer: Understanding matter (what pollutants are) and energy (what can remove them) allows chemists to design and test systems that make water safe.

procedureExamples.prompt: Describe one example of chemistry happening in your body right now.
steps: Step 1: Your body breaks down food into simpler substances—that's a **chemical reaction**.
Step 2: **Energy** from those reactions powers your muscles and brain.
Step 3: **Matter** (atoms) is rearranged to build new cells and repair old ones.
Step 4: The scope of chemistry in medicine relies on understanding these processes.
procedureExamples.answer: Digestion is a series of chemical reactions that convert food (matter) into energy and building blocks your body needs.

worksheet.title: Chemistry and You: First-Day Thinking
worksheet.instructions: This is a **no-grade** reflection to help you and me understand where you're starting. Answer in complete sentences or with examples. Work alone or with a partner—just show your thinking.

sections.directions: Directions: Match each term to the best example. Then briefly explain why it matches.
sections.workedExample:
**Example:** Term: **Energy**. Example: *a candle burning brightly*. Why: The heat and light from the candle show energy being released during a chemical reaction.

*(You'll match three terms to three examples.)*
problems: **Term: Matter.** Examples: (A) a bottle of water, (B) a sunset, (C) courage. Match and explain why.
**Term: Chemical change.** Examples: (A) melting ice, (B) rust forming on a nail, (C) a ball rolling downhill. Match and explain why.
**Term: Scope of chemistry.** Examples: (A) drawing a picture, (B) developing a new plastic that breaks down faster, (C) learning history. Match and explain why.

sections.directions: Directions: Answer in 1–3 sentences. Use your own words.
sections.workedExample: **Example prompt:** Why might a farmer care about chemistry? **Example answer:** A farmer cares about chemistry because it explains how soil nutrients feed plants, how pesticides work to protect crops, and how to grow food sustainably without harming the environment.
problems: Where do you see or use chemistry in your daily life? Give one real example.
🌶 A doctor prescribes an antibiotic when you have a bacterial infection. Using what you learned today, explain why chemists had to study atoms and molecules to create that medicine.
If you heat sugar in a pan until it turns brown, is that a physical change or a chemical change? Explain your reasoning.

sections.directions: Directions: Think about yourself as a learner in this class.
sections.workedExample: **Example prompt:** What is one thing you hope to learn this year in chemistry? **Example answer:** I hope to understand why reactions happen and maybe see them in labs—I think experiments are cool and want to know the science behind them.
problems: What is one reason you're taking this class? (No wrong answer—be honest.)
Name one place or field where chemistry might be important in the future (medicine, sports, art, cooking, fixing a car, etc.).

procedure: Read each prompt carefully.
Write your answer in complete sentences or bullet points—show your thinking.
If you're unsure, make a good guess; there are no 'wrong' answers on this first day.
Raise your hand if you need clarification, but don't ask me for the answer.
optionalExtra: 🌶 **Challenge:** A company wants to design a new material for phone screens that is stronger and more environmentally friendly. Explain which of the four pillars of chemistry (matter, energy, change, applications) they would need to understand, and why.

exitTicket: In one sentence: What is chemistry, and where do you see it happening?

answers: **Term: Matter.** Correct match: **(A) a bottle of water.** Explanation: Water is a substance that has mass and takes up space; it is matter. (B and C are incorrect: a sunset is light/energy; courage is an emotion.)

**Term: Chemical change.** Correct match: **(B) rust forming on a nail.** Explanation: Rust is a new substance formed when iron reacts with oxygen in air; the original metal has changed into something chemically different. (A is physical change—ice returns to water; C is motion, not change.)

**Term: Scope of chemistry.** Correct match: **(B) developing a new plastic that breaks down faster.** Explanation: This requires knowledge of molecular structure and reactions—core topics in chemistry. (A is art; C is history.)

Answers will vary. Examples: cooking (heat breaks apart food molecules), brushing teeth (fluoride in toothpaste prevents decay), taking medicine (drugs work because of how they interact with molecules in your body), charging a phone (battery uses chemical reactions to make electricity). Credit any genuine, chemistry-related observation.

**Challenge:** An antibiotic kills bacteria because chemists understood the structure of bacterial cells at the atomic and molecular level. They designed a molecule that fits into and disrupts a specific part of the bacterial cell—something that doesn't exist in human cells. This required studying **matter** (atoms and molecules) and **change** (how molecules interact), making it a direct **application** of chemistry in **medicine**.

**Chemical change.** When sugar heats, the molecules break apart and recombine into new substances (caramel is not the same as sugar—it has different properties and cannot easily be reversed). A physical change would be melting (solid to liquid, but still sugar).

Answers will vary. Examples: 'I want to understand how medicines work,' 'I'm curious about reactions and what happens when things mix,' 'My parent works in a science field and I want to know what they do,' 'I like problem-solving and thinking about how things work.' Credit any honest response that shows engagement.

Answers will vary. Examples: medicine (drugs), cooking (recipes), environmental cleanup (pollution), sports (energy in muscles), art (pigments and reactions). Credit any genuine application of chemistry.

**Answer:** The company would need to understand all four pillars: **Matter** (atoms and bonds in the material's structure—what makes it strong?), **Energy** (how much heat or light the material can withstand), **Change** (how quickly it breaks down in the environment—can it decompose safely?), and **Applications** (will it work in a real phone and benefit users without harming Earth?). The material science requires balancing strength with sustainability, which relies on deep chemistry knowledge.

script.title: Finalize and sign Core 4 poster

script.title: Play video
script.do: Show the short video on lab safety equipment and procedures. Cue students to pay attention to standing position, equipment handling, and safety gear.

Pause the video halfway through and ask one of the four video questions to check understanding.

script.title: Teacher demo: standing position and equipment care
script.do: Demonstrate the correct standing position at the lab bench (feet shoulder-width apart, side-on to the bench, goggles on). Then show proper handling: picking up a beaker, setting it down, cleaning and storing it.
options: Invite a student volunteer to model one action (e.g., picking up equipment) while you narrate.
If no lab bench is available, use a table or desk and emphasize the same principles.
script.say: Stand like this: feet apart, not too close to the bench. Goggles on before you touch anything. When you pick up a beaker, hold it firmly but not squeezed. Always clean and put it back in the same spot. Why? So the next person knows where it is and can trust it's clean.

script.title: Group practice: standing position and equipment care
script.do: Pair students. One student practices standing at a lab bench or table in the correct position while the partner observes and gives feedback using a simple checklist (goggles on, feet apart, side-on, hand position). Swap roles. Then both practice picking up, using, and storing a piece of equipment (e.g., a beaker, test tube, or stirring rod). Circulate and correct.
options: If space is limited, do a whole-class slow-motion demo: you call out the steps, everyone does them together.
Use a 'fishbowl' model: one pair performs while the others observe and comment.
script.say: Let's practice together. Get into your pair. One of you stands at the bench — let's see that correct position. Partner, you'll watch for: goggles on, feet apart, side-on stance. Then you swap. We want this to be automatic so you can focus on the chemistry, not the mechanics.

script.title: Co-create lab-safety anchor chart
script.do: Gather the class in front of a large blank poster or whiteboard. Title it 'Lab Safety: Our Core Agreements.' Facilitate a discussion: What did you learn from the video and demo? What safety rules do we need? Record student ideas in categories: (1) Personal Protective Equipment, (2) Standing & Positioning, (3) Equipment Care, (4) Spills & Breaks, (5) When in Doubt, Ask. Add visuals (simple drawings or icons the teacher or a student sketch) and finalize the anchor chart. Post it in the lab and classroom.
options: Assign small groups to draft one section each, then assemble them together.
Print a template anchor chart with blank sections and have pairs fill in the content.
script.say: What did you see in the video that surprised you? What do you already do at home that's similar? Let's turn your ideas into rules that make the lab a safe place for everyone.

script.do: Distribute exit-ticket slips. Students write their answer to one prompt.

Tue.notes:
## Key Idea
Lab safety is built on respect for equipment, clear procedures, and commitment from every person in the room. Today you're learning two foundational procedures and signing a commitment to norms that protect everyone.

## Key Terms
- **Personal protective equipment (PPE):** gear like safety goggles, aprons, and gloves that protect your body from chemicals and heat.
- **Standing position:** the correct way to stand at a lab bench — feet shoulder-width apart, side-on, eyes and hands at the right height.
- **Equipment care:** cleaning, handling, and storing lab equipment so it's safe to use and available for others.

## Procedure: Correct Standing Position
**Step 1:** Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, one foot slightly forward.  
**Step 2:** Turn your body sideways to the lab bench so your hip and shoulder point toward it (not straight-on).  
**Step 3:** Keep your goggles on and your hands in front of you, ready to work.  
**Step 4:** Keep your face at a comfortable height above the bench — not too close, not too far.

## Procedure: Equipment Care
**Step 1:** Before you pick up equipment, check that your hands are dry and your goggles are on.  
**Step 2:** Grip firmly but gently — equipment can break if squeezed too hard or dropped.  
**Step 3:** Use equipment only for its purpose (e.g., beakers for liquids, not as hammers).  
**Step 4:** After use, rinse the equipment with water and place it in the correct storage spot.  
**Step 5:** If equipment breaks, tell an adult right away — don't try to fix it or hide it.

## You Try
**Scenario 1:** You walk up to the lab bench. What should you do first, and why?
*Answer:* Put on your goggles. They protect your eyes from splashes and are the first line of defense.

**Scenario 2:** You pick up a beaker. Your friend bumps you. What do you do?
*Answer:* Don't panic. If the beaker is safe, set it down calmly on the bench. If it's broken, tell your teacher right away so no one gets hurt.

formulas.name: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)

formulas.name: Equipment Care

examples.label: Standing Position — the Foundation
examples.prompt: You're about to pour a liquid from a graduated cylinder into a beaker. Show the correct way to stand at the lab bench and explain why each part of your position matters for safety.
steps: Stand with your {{feet shoulder-width apart|4cm}}.
Turn your {{body sideways|2cm}} to the bench — hip and shoulder point toward it.
Put your {{goggles on|2cm}} and keep your hands in front of you.
Keep your {{face at a comfortable height|3cm}} above the bench (not too close).
examples.answer: Correct standing position: feet apart, side-on, goggles on, ready to work.

examples.label: Equipment Care — Respect and Responsibility
examples.prompt: You finish using a stirring rod that has water on it. What do you do to care for it and where do you store it?
steps: Rinse the beaker with {{clean water|2cm}} until no residue remains.
Dry it carefully with a {{paper towel or cloth|3cm}}.
Place it in the {{correct storage spot|3cm}} so the next person can find it.
If it's {{chipped or cracked|3cm}}, tell your teacher — don't use it.
examples.answer: Equipment care: rinse, dry, store in the right place, report damage immediately.

youTry.prompt: You're standing at the lab bench with your goggles on. You just finished rinsing a test tube and your hands are wet. What do you do before setting the test tube down on the bench?
youTry.answer: Dry your hands with a towel first. Wet hands can make equipment slip and break.

youTry.prompt: During an experiment, you notice a strong chemical smell coming from the setup. Walk through the first three actions you take.
youTry.answer: Tell an adult right away. Never ignore unusual smells — they often signal a spill or leak that needs attention.

guidedNotes.summary: Lab safety rests on three pillars: {{wearing PPE at all times|3cm}}, {{using correct standing position|3cm}}, and {{treating equipment with respect|3cm}}. When you follow these, everyone stays safe.

vocab.definition: gear such as safety goggles, lab aprons, and gloves that protect your body from chemicals, heat, and sharp objects in the lab.
the safe, correct way to stand at a lab bench: feet shoulder-width apart, body sideways, goggles on, hands ready to work.
the practice of handling, cleaning, and storing lab equipment safely so it is ready for the next person and free from damage.

slides.heading: Every Safety Rule Has a Story
bullets: Someone once ignored a small spill. It became a big one.
Someone once grabbed hot equipment without looking. It left a burn mark.
Someone once stood straight-on at a bench and couldn't see what they were mixing.
Today, we learn the rules that make sure those stories don't happen here.

slides.heading: What We're Doing Today
bullets: **Finalize & sign** the Core 4 class norms — a real commitment to each other.
**Practice two key procedures:** correct standing position and equipment care.
**Co-create an anchor chart** that reminds us (and the next chemistry class) what safety looks like.
**Take responsibility** for making the lab a place where everyone can focus on chemistry, not worry.

slides.heading: Model: Correct Standing Position at the Lab Bench
bullets: **Feet:** shoulder-width apart, one foot slightly forward (not together, not too wide).
**Body:** turned sideways to the bench, not straight-on. Your hip and shoulder point toward the bench.
**Head & goggles:** on before you touch anything. Eyes level with the work, not too close.
**Hands:** ready in front of you, dry, not in pockets or crossed.

slides.heading: Model: Equipment Care — Clean, Handle, Store
bullets: **Before:** goggles on, hands dry, eyes on what you're doing.
**During:** grip firmly but gently. A beaker is a tool, not a toy. Use it only for its purpose.
**After:** rinse with water, dry, return to the correct shelf or drawer **immediately**.
**If it breaks:** tell an adult at once. Broken glass can cut; a chemical spill can harm. No exceptions.

slides.heading: Common Mistake: 'It's Just a Little Spill'
bullets: A tiny spill can evaporate, spread, or mix with something else — you won't know until it's bigger.
A small broken piece of glass can cut someone later.
**Right move:** report it immediately. Let the adult assess. Your honesty keeps everyone safe and solves problems fast.

vocab.definition: gear like goggles, aprons, and gloves that shield your body from chemicals and heat.
feet apart, body sideways to the bench, goggles on — the foundation for safe lab work.
cleaning, handling, and storing lab tools so they stay safe and available for others.

slides.heading: Your Path Today (and into the Lab)
bullets: **1. Bell ringer & norms recap** — remember yesterday's Core 4 agreements.
**2. Sign the poster** — you're pledging to uphold these norms.
**3. Watch & discuss the video** — lab safety in action.
**4. Practice together** — standing position and equipment care (pairs).
**5. Co-create the anchor chart** — turn your learning into a class resource.
**6. Exit ticket** — one safety rule you'll keep with you.

procedureExamples.prompt: You're about to observe a reaction in a beaker. Demonstrate the correct standing position at the lab bench—show where your feet go, which direction your body faces, and where your goggles sit. Explain why each detail protects you.
steps: Step 1: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Why? This gives you balance and stability so you don't bump the bench or lean into it.
Step 2: Turn sideways to the bench (not straight-on). Why? You can see over the workspace better, and if something splashes, it doesn't hit your eyes or face straight-on.
Step 3: Put on your goggles before you touch anything. Why? Eyes are the easiest target for a splash — once a chemical hits your eye, you can't undo it in seconds.
Step 4: Keep hands in front of you, dry and ready. Why? Wet hands slip. Hands that know where to go keep you in control.
procedureExamples.answer: Correct standing position: feet apart, body sideways, goggles on, hands ready. Each choice protects a different part of your body and keeps you in control.

procedureExamples.prompt: After an experiment, you have used a graduated cylinder, a test tube that was heated, and a glass rod. Walk through the care and cleaning steps for each piece, explaining why timing and thoroughness matter.
steps: Step 1: Before you move anything, check what was in each tool. Rinse the beaker with water, and use a test-tube brush inside the test tube to remove residue.
Step 2: Rinse all three pieces thoroughly under running water. Any chemical left behind can react with the next experiment or corrode the glass over time.
Step 3: Dry each piece with a paper towel or cloth. This prevents water spots and makes sure they're ready for the next use.
Step 4: Return each piece to its marked shelf or drawer. If something is broken or doesn't look right, set it aside and tell your teacher — don't put damaged equipment back.
procedureExamples.answer: Equipment care: rinse thoroughly, dry completely, return to the correct place. If something is damaged, report it and don't put it back.

worksheet.title: Lab Safety & Procedures: Understanding & Application
worksheet.instructions: This worksheet is a **recap and reflection** on what you learned today. There are no calculations or long answer keys — instead, you're thinking about WHY safety rules matter and HOW you'll follow them in the lab. Answer each question in the space provided. You do not need to write in complete sentences; bullet points and short phrases are fine.

sections.workedExample: **Example:** Look at the side-view diagram of correct standing position. Label: (a) the distance between the feet, (b) the angle of the body relative to the bench, (c) where the goggles are, (d) where the hands are. *Answer:* (a) shoulder-width apart; (b) sideways (perpendicular or 90°); (c) on the eyes; (d) in front, ready to work.
sections.directions: Directions: Examine the diagram of the lab bench and the student. Label or describe each part of the correct standing position.

problems: Label the diagram: Mark where the feet should be (A), how far apart (B), where the goggles go (C), and the direction the body faces relative to the bench (D).
Why is standing sideways (not straight-on) better for safety in the lab?
If you're standing correctly and someone bumps into you, what part of your body is LEAST likely to hit the bench or equipment? Why?

sections.workedExample: **Example:** You finish using a beaker in which you mixed two solutions. Describe the correct care sequence. *Answer:* (1) Rinse the inside and outside with tap water to remove all residue. (2) Use a cloth or paper towel to dry it completely. (3) Return it to the beaker shelf in its proper spot. (4) If any crack or chip is visible, set it aside and tell the teacher. Each step ensures the beaker is safe for the next person and ready to use.
sections.directions: Directions: For each scenario, describe what you would do to care for the equipment properly.
problems: After heating a liquid in a test tube, the test tube is still warm. What steps do you take to care for it, and why must you wait before handling it?
🌶 You notice a small chip on the rim of a beaker. Some students say 'It's tiny — it's fine to use.' Why is reporting this to your teacher the right move, even though it seems small?
You use a stirring rod to mix chemicals. When you're done, the rod has sticky residue on it. Describe how you clean it and where you store it.
If you accidentally break a piece of glassware, what is the FIRST thing you tell your teacher — and why is honesty more important than worry?

sections.workedExample: **Example:** You see a small puddle of an unknown chemical on the bench next to the equipment someone was using. What do you do? *Answer:* (1) Do not touch it or try to clean it. (2) Move away and tell an adult right away. (3) Describe where the spill is and what equipment was nearby. (4) Follow your teacher's instructions. Why: You don't know what the chemical is, how it will react if touched or mixed with something else, or whether it's safe. The adult can assess and handle it correctly.
sections.directions: Directions: For each safety situation, decide what YOU would do. Write your answer and explain your reasoning.
problems: You smell a sharp or unusual odor during an experiment. What do you do?
Your lab partner is standing straight-on to the bench, leaning toward the equipment. What do you say to them?
🌶 Two students are racing to see who finishes their equipment care first. One is rushing and doesn't rinse carefully. How do you respond, and why does speed not matter in the lab?
You're cleaning up and find a wet paper towel on the floor near the bench. What do you do?

procedure: Read the scenario or question carefully.
Think about the safety rule or procedure that applies.
Write your answer — explain your reasoning when asked.
If you're unsure, refer to the guided notes or the anchor chart you created today.
optionalExtra: 🌶 **Challenge:** Imagine you're teaching a new student the rules of lab safety for the first time. Write two paragraphs: one about standing position and why it matters, and one about equipment care. Pretend you're explaining to someone who has never been in a lab before.

**Challenge:** Look at the Core 4 class norms you signed today. Write one sentence for each norm explaining how it applies in the lab. For example: 'Respect' in the lab means treating equipment and shared space as if they belong to everyone.

extension.title: Challenge — Design Your Own Lab Safety Poster
extension.prompt: Choose one lab safety procedure (standing position, equipment care, or spill protocol). Create a simple one-page poster or infographic that teaches that procedure to someone who has never been in a lab. Include: a title, 3–4 key steps, and either a labeled diagram or simple drawings. (You can draw it on the back of this worksheet or on a separate sheet.)
extension.why: This extends your understanding by asking you to teach others — you have to know the procedure well enough to explain it clearly and visually.

exitTicket: What is one safety procedure you will follow EVERY TIME you enter the lab, and why does it matter?
Name one piece of safety equipment and describe what it protects.

answers: **Problem 1 (Diagram labels):** A = Left foot; B = Right foot (or: feet shoulder-width apart); C = Goggles (on the eyes); D = Body sideways/perpendicular to the bench (or: facing away from the straight-on direction). Each label shows one part of the correct standing position.

**Problem 2:** Standing sideways protects your face and eyes. If a splash occurs, it's less likely to hit your eyes directly; your body also gives you room to step back quickly without tripping over the bench or bumping into it.

**Problem 3:** Your back or the back of your body is least likely to hit the bench or equipment because your front (where your hands, face, and eyes are) is turned away from the bench. This is why standing sideways protects the most vulnerable parts.

**Problem 4 (Spill smell):** Stop what you're doing and tell an adult right away. Unusual smells often signal a spill, leak, or chemical reaction that needs immediate attention. Never ignore a smell or assume it's harmless.

**Problem 1 (Warm test tube care):** (1) Let the test tube cool on the bench for 2–3 minutes (or ask your teacher how long). (2) Once cool, rinse the inside with a test-tube brush and tap water to remove all residue. (3) Rinse the outside. (4) Dry completely with a paper towel. (5) Return to the test-tube rack in its spot. Why wait: Hot glass can burn your hands and cause you to drop it, breaking it and losing control of what's inside.

**Problem 2 (Chipped beaker — Challenge):** Even a small chip creates a sharp edge that can cut skin during use or storage. It can also weaken the glass, causing it to crack or shatter under heat or pressure. Reporting it immediately prevents injury and allows the school to replace it before someone gets hurt. Honesty builds trust and keeps everyone safe.

**Problem 3 (Stirring rod with residue):** (1) Soak the rod briefly in tap water if the residue is sticky. (2) Rub it gently with a cloth or brush to remove all residue. (3) Rinse thoroughly under running water. (4) Dry with a paper towel. (5) Place in the stirring-rod container or drawer. The residue can stick to the next person's hands or react with a different chemical if left on.

**Problem 4 (Broken glassware — honesty):** The first thing to tell your teacher is: 'I broke a [piece of equipment] in the lab. I'm sorry.' Why honesty is crucial: (a) The teacher needs to know right away so they can assess the spill or broken pieces and prevent injury. (b) Hiding it puts the next person at risk. (c) Honesty builds trust. (d) The teacher is not angry — they want to help, not punish. Reporting immediately is the right move every time.

**Problem 1 (Unusual odor):** (1) Stop your experiment immediately. (2) Move away from the bench and tell an adult right away. (3) Describe what you were doing and where the smell is coming from. (4) Follow your teacher's instructions. Do not try to figure out the smell or fix it yourself. Unusual odors can indicate a spill, a dangerous reaction, or an irritant that can harm your lungs or eyes.

**Problem 2 (Partner standing straight-on):** Say: 'You should turn sideways — you'll see better and it's safer if something splashes.' (Or: ask them to fix their position.) Explain: This is not rude; it's caring about your partner's safety. Everyone in the lab is responsible for keeping everyone else safe.

**Problem 3 (Racing through cleanup — Challenge):** You could say: 'Slow down — the point is that equipment is clean and ready for the next person, not that we finish first.' Speed in the lab leads to mistakes: incomplete rinsing, spilled chemicals, broken equipment, and dishonesty (skipping steps). In chemistry, slow and careful beats fast and sloppy every time.

**Problem 4 (Wet paper towel on floor):** Pick it up carefully (using a fresh paper towel if needed) and put it in the trash. A wet towel on the floor is a slip hazard and looks messy. Keeping the lab clean is everyone's job, not just the person who used that station.

Wed.hook: You've learned procedures, made norms, and thought about safety. Today you become safety ambassadors—and take a short diagnostic to show me what you already know about chemistry.
Wed.objective: Students will finalize the lab-safety anchor chart, complete a low-stakes beginning-of-year diagnostic (TEKS-tagged: 112.43(c)(1).C, D; 112.43(c)(3).B; 112.43(c)(4).B), and reflect on what they're curious about in chemistry.

Finalize and post the 'Safety First' anchor chart
Teach Procedure 5: Transition to group work & using the lab (brief visual tour of the lab space)
Low-stakes beginning-of-year diagnostic (15–18 min, ~10 items covering observation, measurement, safety, atoms)
Informal check (3–4 min quiz-style: spot a safety hazard, identify a basic lab tool, state what 'evidence' means)

script.title: Bell ringer & sharing
script.do: Display the bell-ringer prompt. As students enter and work, circulate and read a few answers aloud. Affirm curiosity: 'That's a great question—we're going to explore that this year.' Collect the index cards and save them (use later in Week 2 to connect to content).
options: Create a 'Chemistry Questions Wall' and post student questions throughout the unit.
Pick one question and say, 'Let's come back to this in two weeks and see if we can answer it together.'
script.say: I love these questions. Keep asking them. That's what real scientists do.

script.title: Finalize and post the 'Safety First' anchor chart
script.do: Bring back the draft from Tue. Add any new items the class thinks of in 1 min. Format it neatly, highlight key phrases, and hang it near the lab entrance or next to the norms poster. Say: 'This chart is our safety contract, written in our own words. Every time you walk into the lab, you're going to remember these five things.'
options: Have students vote on the 'most important' safety rule and circle it in a bright color.
Create a laminated 'Safety Checklist' card (one per student) to keep at their lab station.
script.say: Look at what we've built this week: norms, procedures, and a safety mindset. You're already acting like chemists.

script.title: Teach Procedure 5: Transition to group work & lab tour
script.do: Explain: 'By next week, you'll be doing hands-on labs. That means working in groups and using the lab safely and efficiently.' Do a 3-min visual tour of the lab space (or the area where small experiments will happen). Point out: storage cabinets, sink, disposal containers, fire extinguisher, eyewash station, goggles bin. Say: 'When you enter the lab area, you're putting on goggles. When you're done, you check with your group leader that everything is clean and returned.' Introduce roles: Lab Leader (checks safety), Data Recorder (writes observations), Equipment Manager (collects and returns tools), and Communicator (shares results). Say: 'You'll rotate roles each lab so everyone gets practice at every job.'
options: Have a student volunteer be the 'tour guide' and show their classmates the lab.
Post a laminated 'Lab Roles' card at each lab station.
script.say: The lab is a team space. Each role matters. Next week, you'll get your group and your first role.

script.title: Low-stakes beginning-of-year diagnostic
script.do: Hand out or project the diagnostic (see 'Diagnostic' section below). Say: 'This isn't a test. I'm just curious about what you already know. Do your best, and if you're not sure, make a thoughtful guess or write "I'm not sure yet." This helps me know where to start.' Read the instructions aloud. Set a timer for 15–18 min. As students work, circulate, offer encouragement, and do NOT correct. Collect at the end.
options: Pair struggling readers with a peer buddy to read questions aloud (not to answer for them).
Break the diagnostic into two parts (10 min + 8 min) with a 1-min stretch in between.
script.say: Take your time. There are no trick questions. Show me what you're thinking.

script.title: Informal check: mid-week mastery quiz
script.do: After collecting diagnostics, project 4 quick items (a 2-min verbal or written check): (1) 'Name one piece of safety equipment you'd use in a chemistry lab.' (2) 'What does it mean to observe something in science?' (3) 'Point to the area on the board where we post lab norms.' (4) 'If you spill water in the lab, what's your first step?' Take oral responses or have students write answers on whiteboards. Use this to gauge readiness and group students for small-group support.
options: Turn it into a quick game: first person to answer correctly gets a point for their group.
Have students self-assess: 'Which of these four are you confident about? Raise your hand for each one.'
script.say: Let's check what's clear and what we need to practice more.

script.title: Debrief diagnostic & celebrate
script.do: Say: 'You all did great. I saw some smart thinking out there. Here's what I noticed: you know a lot about safety already, and some of you are curious about atoms and reactions. Over this year, we're going to answer all those questions.' Highlight one thing you observed from the diagnostics that showed growth or insight (e.g., 'A lot of you said you want to know what makes a fire—that's chemistry!').
options: Return the diagnostic to students and have them highlight their best answer.
Share one surprising or clever answer (anonymously) and have the class appreciate it.
script.say: You're ready for real chemistry. This week we built the foundation. Next week, we go deeper.

script.title: Exit ticket & closing
script.do: Hand out the exit ticket. Give 2 min. Collect as students leave.
options: Use a digital form.
Have students share one word that describes how they felt this week (excited, ready, curious, etc.).
script.say: Reflect on this week: What was one thing you learned about being a good lab partner or scientist?

worksheet.title: Beginning-of-Year Diagnostic: Chemistry Awareness
worksheet.instructions: This is NOT a test. It shows what you already know. Do your best. If you're unsure, make a thoughtful guess or write 'I'm not sure yet.'

sections.why: These questions check that you can recognize safe behavior and notice details—two core lab skills.
sections.directions: Directions: Answer each question in 1–2 sentences.
problems: Look at the picture of the lab (shown on the board or handout). Name two pieces of safety equipment you see.
If you see someone running in the hallway toward the lab, is that safe or unsafe? Explain why.
What does the word 'observe' mean in science? Give an example.

sections.why: These questions check your prior knowledge about the tiniest scale of chemistry—atoms and simple particles.
sections.directions: Directions: Answer in 1–2 sentences or draw a quick picture.
problems: Have you ever heard the word 'atom'? If yes, what do you think an atom is?
If you have a cup of water and a cup of salt, which one is made of atoms? Why?
If you break a piece of chalk in half, and keep breaking it smaller and smaller, do you think you'll eventually get to a piece so tiny nothing can break it further? Why or why not?

sections.why: These items assess whether you understand that science uses measurements and evidence, not just opinions.
sections.directions: Directions: Choose the best answer or explain your thinking.
problems: A scientist wants to know how fast a ball rolls down a ramp. Should they (a) guess, (b) measure the distance and time, or (c) ask a friend? Why?
If you feel a piece of metal and it feels cold, is that enough evidence to say metal is always cold? Explain.
What does the word 'evidence' mean in science?

procedure: Read each question carefully.
Write your best answer. If you're not sure, make a thoughtful guess or write 'I'm not sure yet.'
Use complete sentences when you can.
Don't worry about spelling or perfect grammar—just show your thinking.

exitTicket: Reflection: What was one thing you learned about yourself this week as a lab partner or student? (1–2 sentences)

answers: Acceptable answers: goggles, gloves, fire extinguisher, eyewash station, apron, closed-toe shoes, lab coat. (Any two correct items.)

Unsafe. Explanation should mention: running is dangerous in a lab because (a) you might bump into equipment, (b) you could spill chemicals, (c) you might fall, or (d) it shows you're not in control. Accept any safe reasoning.
Observe means to notice details using your senses (eyes, ears, maybe touch carefully). Example: watching how a candle flame changes color or listening to how ice cracks as it melts.

Accept any attempt: 'An atom is the smallest piece of something,' 'It's a tiny thing made of even tinier things,' 'Everything is made of atoms.' Do not require perfect accuracy—this is a baseline check.
Both are made of atoms. Water is H₂O (atoms bonded together), and salt is NaCl (atoms bonded together). Accept reasoning like 'Everything is made of atoms' or 'Both are matter.'
Yes, there's eventually a smallest piece (the atom). Accept reasoning about a limit, or accept 'I think it keeps going.' This is open-ended baseline; perfect answer not expected.

What's the evidence?' Collect observations aloud (fizzing, bubbles, color, heat). Say: 'All of that is evidence of a chemical reaction. New substances formed. script.title: Independent practice: Sketch, label, and describe the reaction

Thu.notes:
## Chemical Reactions

### Key Idea
A **chemical reaction** is when one or more substances interact and form a new substance with different properties. You can tell a reaction happened by observing **evidence**: color changes, bubbles or fizzing, heat, light, or a new smell.

### Key Terms
**Reaction**: a process where matter changes into a new form with new properties.
**Observation**: something you notice using your senses (eyes, ears, touch, sometimes smell).
**Evidence**: facts or data you collect from observations; in science, evidence supports your explanation.

### Worked Example: Baking Soda + Vinegar
**Step 1**: Start with white baking-soda powder in a clear cup.
**Step 2**: Add a few drops of red food coloring.
**Step 3**: Pour in vinegar slowly.
**Step 4**: Observe. The mixture fizzes (bubbles form and rise), foams, changes color, and may feel warm.
**Step 5**: Explanation. A chemical reaction happened because new substances formed with new properties (bubbles, foam, color, warmth). These are signs that atoms rearranged.

### You Try
**Prompt**: If you mix baking soda and vinegar in a sealed bag, it puffs up and gets cold. Using what you know about reactions, what is the evidence that a chemical reaction happened? What does each piece of evidence tell you?

**Answer**: Evidence: (1) The bag puffs up → gas is forming (atoms rearranged to make a new substance). (2) It gets cold → energy left the reaction (exothermic *or* the bag is cold because energy is absorbed—this is exploratory, and either answer shows thinking). (3) You hear a sound → the gas pressure inside changed. Each piece of evidence points to a new substance forming, which is a sign of a chemical reaction.

youTry.prompt: You burn a piece of paper in a dish. You observe smoke rising, the paper turning black, and heat. Is this a chemical reaction? What is your evidence?
youTry.answer: Yes, it is a chemical reaction. The substance didn't change into something new; it just spread out. No new substance formed, so no chemical reaction.

slides.heading: Watch Out: Not All Changes Are Chemical Reactions
bullets: **Dissolving sugar in water**: Sugar disappears, but it's still sugar (just mixed in). No new substance. NOT a reaction.

Yes, a chemical reaction happened because new substances formed with different properties. The starting materials (white powder + liquid) became a foam, bubbles, and a colored mixture—all new substances.

## Describing Chemical Reactions

### Key Idea
When you observe a chemical reaction, describe it carefully: what you see (observation), what it means (interpretation), and why it proves a reaction happened (explanation using evidence). Precise language and step-by-step thinking show Quality of Work.

### Key Terms
**Reactant**: the starting substance(s).
**Product**: the new substance(s) formed.
**Observable evidence**: color change, bubbles/fizzing, heat, light, new texture or smell.

### Worked Example: Burning Paper
**Observation**: A piece of paper is lit with a flame. It turns black, crumbles into ash, and smoke rises.
**Interpretation**: The black color and ash show new substances formed. Smoke is a gas (new substance).
**Explanation**: This is a chemical reaction because the paper atoms rearranged into new substances (ash, gases, heat, light). The evidence is clear: color change (black), new texture (ash), and visible smoke (gas).

### You Try
**Scenario**: You mix baking soda (white powder) and vinegar (clear liquid). Fizzing happens, and the mixture feels warm. Describe this reaction. Is it a chemical reaction? Why?

**Answer**: Observation: fizzing, warmth, foam forming. Interpretation: New substances are forming (the gas is CO₂, the foam is a new product). Explanation: Yes, this is a chemical reaction because atoms rearranged. Evidence: (1) fizzing = gas formed (new substance), (2) warmth = energy involved, (3) foam = new texture (new substance). All observations prove new substances formed.

slides.heading: Three-Step Description of a Reaction
bullets: **Step 1 — Observe**: Describe what you see, hear, feel. Use precise words: color, texture, motion, heat, sound.

bullets: **Observe**: An iron nail left in water for a week turns orange and flaky. It's no longer shiny.

Mon.notes:
## Key Idea
Scientists worldwide use the **SI (International System of Units)** so that measurements are universally understood. Every measurement has a **number** and a **unit** — without the unit, the number is meaningless.

## Key Terms
- **SI base unit** — a fundamental, defined unit from which all others are derived (e.g., meter, kilogram, second)
- **Metric prefix** — a word part added to a base unit to indicate a power of ten (e.g., kilo- = 1000×, milli- = 0.001×)
- **Accuracy** — how close a measurement is to the TRUE (accepted) value
- **Precision** — how close REPEATED measurements are to EACH OTHER (reproducibility)
- **Quantitative data** — data expressed as a NUMBER with a unit (e.g., 25.3 mL)
- **Qualitative data** — data expressed as a DESCRIPTION without numbers (e.g., "the solution turned blue")

## SI Base Units Table
| Quantity | SI Base Unit | Symbol |
|----------|-------------|--------|
| Length | meter | m |
| Mass | kilogram | kg |
| Time | second | s |
| Temperature | kelvin | K |
| Amount of substance | mole | mol |
| Electric current | ampere | A |
| Luminous intensity | candela | cd |

## Common Metric Prefixes
| Prefix | Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|--------|---------|
| kilo- | k | × 1000 |
| centi- | c | × 0.01 |
| milli- | m | × 0.001 |
| micro- | μ | × 0.000001 |

## Worked Example — Prefix Identification
A nurse records a patient's mass as 68 kg. What quantity is being measured, and what does the prefix tell you?

**Step 1:** Identify the base unit → *kilogram* → base unit is **gram** (g), which measures **mass**.

**Step 2:** Identify the prefix → *kilo-* means **1000 ×**.

**Answer:** Mass is measured; 68 kg = 68 × 1000 g = 68,000 g.

## Worked Example — Accuracy vs Precision
A balance reads 5.02 g, 5.03 g, and 5.02 g for a sample whose true mass is 8.00 g. Are these measurements accurate? Precise?

**Step 1:** Precision → measurements are clustered (5.02, 5.03, 5.02) → **precise** ✓

**Step 2:** Accuracy → measurements average ≈ 5.02 g, but true value = 8.00 g → **NOT accurate** ✗

**Answer:** Precise but not accurate.

## You Try
A thermometer reads $99.1°C$, $99.2°C$, and $99.1°C$ for boiling water. The accepted boiling point is $100.0°C$. Are the readings accurate, precise, both, or neither? Explain in one sentence.

slides.heading: A $327-Million Mistake
bullets: 1999: NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter burned up entering Mars's atmosphere.
Cause: one engineering team used metric units (Newtons), another used imperial units (pound-force) — they never agreed.
The spacecraft had traveled 669 million km and was destroyed by a unit mismatch.
Today's goal: master the ONE unit system scientists use worldwide — SI.

slides.heading: The 7 SI Base Units
bullets: SI = Système International — adopted worldwide so all scientists share a language.
There are exactly 7 base units; all other units are DERIVED from these.
meter (m) — length | kilogram (kg) — mass | second (s) — time
kelvin (K) — temperature | mole (mol) — amount | ampere (A) — current | candela (cd) — light
Memory tip: 'My King Shall Taste More Apple Cider' (m, kg, s, K, mol, A, cd)

vocab.definition: A fundamental, internationally defined unit of measurement — one of only 7.

slides.heading: Metric Prefixes — Scaling the Base Unit
bullets: Prefixes tell you HOW MANY base units you have — they multiply by a power of 10.
kilo- (k): × 1000 → 1 kilometer = 1000 meters
centi- (c): × 0.01 → 1 centimeter = 0.01 meters
milli- (m): × 0.001 → 1 milliliter = 0.001 liters
micro- (μ): × 0.000001 → 1 microgram = 0.000001 grams
Pattern: the prefix NEVER changes — only the base unit does (kilogram, kilometer, kiloliter…)

slides.heading: Worked Example — Reading a Prefix
bullets: Problem: A syringe holds 2.5 mL of medicine. What quantity is measured, and what does the prefix mean?
Step 1: Base unit → liter (L) → measures VOLUME.
Step 2: Prefix → milli- (m) → × 0.001.
Answer: volume; 2.5 mL = 0.0025 L
slides.example:
1. Base unit: liter → Volume
2. Prefix: milli- → ×0.001
3. 2.5 mL = 0.0025 L

slides.heading: Accuracy vs Precision — The Target Model
bullets: ACCURACY: how close your measurement is to the TRUE (bull's-eye) value.
PRECISION: how close your REPEATED measurements are to EACH OTHER.
You can be precise but inaccurate (all shots grouped — but in the wrong spot).
You can be accurate but imprecise (average is correct — but shots are scattered).
GOAL in the lab: both accurate AND precise.

slides.heading: Common Mistake — Confusing Accuracy and Precision
bullets: ❌ Wrong thinking: 'My measurements are all the same, so they must be right (accurate).'
✓ Correct thinking: Consistency = precision; closeness to TRUE value = accuracy.
Example: A broken scale consistently reads 1.5 kg too heavy — PRECISE but NOT accurate.
Always ask: 'Do I know the accepted value?' If yes, compare to it (accuracy). If comparing repeats to each other, that is precision.
slides.mistake: Saying consistent = correct. Consistency only proves precision, NOT accuracy.

procedureExamples.prompt: A doctor records that a newborn has a mass of 3.2 kg. (a) What SI base unit is used? (b) What does the prefix 'kilo-' mean? (c) Convert 3.2 kg to grams.
steps: Step 1 — Identify base unit: kilogram → base unit is GRAM (g); measures MASS.
Step 2 — Identify prefix: kilo- means × 1000.
Step 3 — Convert: 3.2 kg × 1000 g/kg = 3200 g.
procedureExamples.answer: SI base unit = kilogram; kilo- = ×1000; 3.2 kg = 3200 g

procedureExamples.prompt: A student measures the length of a pencil four times and records: 18.2 cm, 18.3 cm, 18.2 cm, 18.3 cm. The accepted length is 19.0 cm. Evaluate the accuracy and precision of these measurements.
steps: Step 1 — Precision: values range from 18.2 to 18.3 cm; variation of only 0.1 cm → measurements ARE precise.
Step 2 — Accuracy: average ≈ 18.25 cm; accepted value = 19.0 cm; difference = 0.75 cm → measurements are NOT accurate.
Step 3 — Conclusion: precise but not accurate (like hitting the same wrong spot on a target every time).
procedureExamples.answer: Precise (clustered) but NOT accurate (consistently below 19.0 cm)

procedureExamples.prompt: Classify each observation: (a) 'The solution turned bright yellow.' (b) 'The temperature increased by 12.4°C.' (c) 'The reaction produced a gas with a sharp odor.'
steps: Step 1 — Ask: does it have a number AND a unit?
(a) 'bright yellow' → description only → QUALITATIVE
(b) '12.4°C' → number + unit → QUANTITATIVE
(c) 'sharp odor' → description only → QUALITATIVE
procedureExamples.answer: (a) qualitative; (b) quantitative; (c) qualitative

procedure: Step 1 — Identify the quantity (length, mass, time, temperature, etc.).
Step 2 — Name the correct SI base unit and its symbol.

Step 4 — Check accuracy by comparing to the true value; check precision by comparing repeated measurements to each other.

6. $2500 \text{ g} \div 1000 = \mathbf{2.5 \text{ kg}}$. (kilo- = ×1000, so divide grams by 1000 to get kilograms.)
7. $0.035 \text{ m} \times 100 = \mathbf{3.5 \text{ cm}}$. (centi- = ×0.01, so 1 m = 100 cm; multiply meters by 100.)

10. $5.0 \text{ km} \times 1000 = \mathbf{5000 \text{ m}}$; $5000 \text{ m} \times 100 = \mathbf{500{,}000 \text{ cm}}$.
11. Prefix: milli- (m), multiplier: ×0.001. $2 \text{ mm} \times 0.001 = \mathbf{0.002 \text{ m}}$.
12. milli- = ×0.001; $9200 \text{ mL} \div 1000 = \mathbf{9.2 \text{ L}}$. The prefix (milli-) is removed and the base unit (liter, L) is kept.

answers: 13. (a) Precise: YES — readings span only 0.02 g (24.97–24.99), tightly clustered. (b) Accurate: YES — average = 24.98 g, very close to the true 25.00 g (difference < 0.1%).
14. (a) Precise: NO — readings range from 87.3°C to 101.8°C, a spread of 14.5°C; not clustered. (b) Accurate: NO — the average ≈ 94.4°C; far from the true 100.0°C.
15. (A) Qualitative — description, no number. (B) Quantitative — 48 mL is a number with a unit. (C) Qualitative — 'shiny, silver' is a description. (D) Quantitative — pH 3.2 is a number.

16. 🌶 The scale is PRECISE (it gives a consistent 2.0 kg error every time — repeatable results) but NOT accurate (readings are always 2.0 kg above the true value). To make it accurate, you would need to recalibrate the scale using a known standard mass so the readings match the true value. Calibration corrects systematic error while preserving precision.

17. The measurements (10.01, 10.00, 10.02 mL) are both PRECISE (spread of only 0.02 mL — tightly grouped) and ACCURATE (average ≈ 10.01 mL, extremely close to the true 10.00 mL), indicating excellent lab technique.

Challenge A: 0.215 km × 1000 m/km = 215 m; 215 m × 100 cm/m = 21,500 cm; 21,500 cm × 10 mm/cm = 215,000 mm. The partner recorded 21,600 cm, which equals 216 m ≠ 215 m — that reading is NOT equal to the others (it is off by 1 m). The third partner's 215,000 mm = 215 m ✓ — equal. Using different units does NOT affect accuracy or precision by itself, but a conversion error (21,600 cm) introduces inaccuracy. One sentence: 'Different unit choices are fine as long as conversions are done correctly; the 21,600 cm reading contains a conversion error and is inaccurate relative to the true distance.'

Challenge B: Accept any three reasonable classroom measurements (e.g., width of a desk, length of a pencil, height of a chair). Precise AND accurate: all three measurements cluster within ±0.1 cm of the true value (verified with a meter stick). Precise but NOT accurate: all three measurements cluster within ±0.1 cm of each other but differ from the true value by 1 cm or more (e.g., consistently measuring only part of the object).

Tue.notes:
## Key Idea
Every measured number contains **significant figures (sig figs)** — the digits that are reliably known plus one estimated digit. More sig figs = more precise instrument. Sig figs tell the reader how trustworthy a measurement is.

---
## Key Terms
- **Significant figure:** a digit that carries meaning about the precision of a measurement.
- **Precision:** how close repeated measurements are to each other; reflected by the number of sig figs.
- **Exact number:** a counted or defined value (e.g., 12 eggs, 1 km = 1000 m) — has **infinite** sig figs; never limits your answer.

---
## The 5 Counting Rules
| Rule | Example | Sig Figs |
|------|---------|----------|
| 1. Non-zero digits always count | 345.6 | 4 |
| 2. Zeros **between** non-zeros count (captive zeros) | 3007 | 4 |
| 3. Leading zeros (before first non-zero) do NOT count | 0.0045 | 2 |
| 4. Trailing zeros **with a decimal point** count | 7.080 | 4 |
| 5. Trailing zeros **without a decimal point** are ambiguous | 3200 | 2 or 4* |

*Use scientific notation to be clear: $3.200 \times 10^3$ = 4 sig figs.

---
## Operations with Sig Figs

**Addition / Subtraction → Round to the fewest DECIMAL PLACES**

Step 1 → Line up decimal points and identify the last reliable decimal place in each number.
Step 2 → Add or subtract normally.
Step 3 → Round the answer to the fewest decimal places of any input.

**Example (add):** $12.11 + 18.0 + 1.013$
- Step 1: $12.11$ ends at hundredths; $18.0$ ends at **tenths** (fewest); $1.013$ ends at thousandths.
- Step 2: $12.11 + 18.0 + 1.013 = 31.123$
- Step 3: Round to tenths → **$31.1$**

---
**Multiplication / Division → Round to the fewest SIG FIG COUNT**

Step 1 → Count sig figs in each measurement.
Step 2 → Multiply or divide normally.
Step 3 → Round the answer to match the input with the fewest sig figs.

**Example (multiply):** $4.56 \times 1.4$
- Step 1: 4.56 has **3** sig figs; 1.4 has **2** sig figs → answer gets **2** sig figs.
- Step 2: $4.56 \times 1.4 = 6.384$
- Step 3: Round to 2 sig figs → **$6.4$**

---
## You Try
How many sig figs are in $0.00580$? Then calculate: $3.21 \times 10^2 \div 1.5$ and express in correct sig figs.

*Answers: $0.00580$ has **3** sig figs (leading zeros don't count; trailing zero after decimal does). $321 \div 1.5 = 214$, but 1.5 has 2 sig figs → **$210$** (2 sig figs).*

formulas.name: Significant figure
formulas.formula: A digit that is reliably known or estimated in a measurement — reflects instrument precision

formulas.name: Captive zero
formulas.formula: A zero between two non-zero digits — ALWAYS significant (e.g., 3007 has 4 sig figs)

formulas.name: Leading zero
formulas.formula: A zero to the LEFT of the first non-zero digit — NEVER significant (just locates the decimal)

formulas.name: Trailing zero
formulas.formula: A zero at the END of a number — counts ONLY when a decimal point is present

formulas.name: Exact number
formulas.formula: A counted or defined quantity with infinite sig figs — never limits an answer

vocab.def: A {{significant figure|2.5cm}} is any digit in a measurement that is known with certainty plus one {{estimated|2cm}} digit.
{{Precision|2cm}} describes how close repeated measurements are; a more precise instrument gives more {{significant figures|2.5cm}}.
An {{exact number|2cm}} comes from counting or a definition; it has {{infinite|1.5cm}} significant figures and never limits your answer's sig figs.

examples.label: Type 1 — Counting significant figures
examples.prompt: How many significant figures are in each: (a) 0.00720  (b) 40500  (c) 9.010 × 10²
steps: 0.00720: leading zeros don't count; 7 and 2 count; trailing zero after decimal {{counts|1.5cm}} → {{3|1cm}} sig figs
40500: trailing zeros with no decimal are {{ambiguous|2cm}}; assume 3 sig figs (4, 0 captive, 5) → {{3|1cm}} sig figs
9.010 × 10²: digits in coefficient only — 9, 0 (captive), 1, 0 (trailing with decimal) → {{4|1cm}} sig figs

examples.label: Type 2 — Addition and Subtraction (decimal places)
examples.prompt: Calculate $25.340 + 6.07 + 103.3$ and report in correct sig figs.
steps: Identify the decimal place of each: 25.340 → thousandths; 6.07 → {{hundredths|2cm}}; 103.3 → {{tenths|2cm}} (fewest)
Round to {{tenths|2cm}} place → {{$134.7$|2cm}}

examples.label: Type 3 — Multiplication and Division (sig fig count)
examples.prompt: Calculate $0.0035 \times 820$ and report in correct sig figs.
steps: Count sig figs: 0.0035 has {{2|1cm}} sig figs; 820 has {{2|1cm}} sig figs → answer: {{2|1cm}} sig figs
Round to 2 sig figs → {{$2.9$|2cm}}

youTry.prompt: How many significant figures are in $0.05080$?
youTry.answer: 3 sig figs: leading zeros don't count; 5 and 8 count; trailing zero after decimal counts.

vocab.definition: Any digit in a measurement that is reliably known plus one estimated digit; reflects the precision of the measuring instrument.
How closely repeated measurements agree with each other; a more precise instrument records more significant figures.
A zero located between two non-zero digits; always significant (e.g., the zero in 3007).
A zero appearing before the first non-zero digit (e.g., 0.0045); never significant — only marks decimal placement.
A zero at the end of a number; significant only when a decimal point is explicitly written (e.g., 7.080 but NOT 3200).
A value obtained by counting discrete items or by definition (e.g., 1 km = 1000 m); has infinite significant figures.

slides.heading: Does Every Digit Matter?
bullets: A bathroom scale reads 68 kg. A hospital scale reads 68.42 kg.
Both are 'correct' — but one tells a doctor much more.
The extra digits aren't random: they reflect HOW PRECISE the instrument is.
Significant figures are the language scientists use to communicate precision.
Bell ringer check: compare your guesses for 0.0045, 3200, and 7.080 — we will revisit these after the rules.

slides.heading: Today's Key Terms
bullets: Significant figure (sig fig): a digit that is reliably known + one estimated digit in a measurement.
Precision: how close repeated measurements are — more sig figs = more precise instrument.
Exact number: a defined or counted value (12 eggs, 1 m = 100 cm) — infinite sig figs, never limits your answer.
Captive zero: zero BETWEEN non-zeros — always counts.
Leading zero: zero BEFORE the first non-zero — never counts (just holds a decimal place).
Trailing zero: zero at the END — counts only when a decimal point is written.

vocab.definition: A reliably-known digit plus one estimated digit in a measurement.
How closely repeated measurements agree; reflected by the number of sig figs.
A counted or defined value; has infinite sig figs.

slides.heading: The 5 Counting Rules — Visual Summary
bullets: Rule 1: Non-zero digits ALWAYS count. → 345.6 has 4 sig figs.
Rule 2: Captive zeros (between non-zeros) ALWAYS count. → 3007 has 4.
Rule 3: Leading zeros NEVER count (placeholders). → 0.0045 has 2.
Rule 4: Trailing zeros WITH a decimal count. → 7.080 has 4.
Rule 5: Trailing zeros WITHOUT a decimal are AMBIGUOUS. → 3200 could be 2, 3, or 4.
Fix ambiguity with scientific notation: 3.200 × 10³ = 4 sig figs.

slides.heading: I Do: Counting Sig Figs Step by Step
bullets: Problem: How many sig figs are in each? (a) 0.00470  (b) 60800  (c) 1.0050 × 10³
Step 1 — Identify any leading zeros and cross them out (they are placeholders only).
Step 2 — Identify captive zeros (between non-zeros) and trailing zeros (check for decimal point).
Step 3 — Count every digit that 'survives' the rules.
slides.example:
1) 0.00470
   Leading zeros (0.00) → cross out → left with 4, 7, 0
   Trailing zero after decimal → COUNTS
   Answer: 3 sig figs
2) 60800
   No decimal point → trailing zeros ambiguous → count 6, 0(captive), 8
   Answer: 3 sig figs
3) 1.0050 × 10³ → only coefficient matters
   1 (non-zero), 0 (captive), 0 (captive), 5, 0 (trailing + decimal)
   Answer: 5 sig figs

slides.heading: I Do: Sig Figs in Add/Subtract and Multiply/Divide
bullets: ADD/SUBTRACT rule: answer has as many DECIMAL PLACES as the measurement with the FEWEST decimal places.
MULTIPLY/DIVIDE rule: answer has as many SIG FIGS as the measurement with the FEWEST sig figs.
Always do the math FIRST, then round at the END — never round mid-calculation.
slides.example:
Addition: 8.925 + 1.73 + 0.5
  8.925 → thousandths; 1.73 → hundredths; 0.5 → tenths (fewest)
  Sum = 11.155
  Round to tenths → 11.2

Multiplication: 2.40 × 15.3
  2.40 has 3 sf; 15.3 has 3 sf → answer: 3 sf
  Product = 36.72 → 36.7

slides.heading: We Do (Group): Apply Both Rules
bullets: Problem A (Counting): How many sig figs are in 300.0? In 0.0002050?
Problem B (Add/Subtract): $5.67 + 0.004 + 12.1 = ?$ → express in correct sig figs.
Problem C (Multiply/Divide): $6.4 \times 10^3 \div 0.68 = ?$ → express in correct sig figs.
Work with your group — one person writes, everyone contributes. We share in 3 minutes.

slides.heading: Common Mistake: Trailing Zeros
bullets: WRONG: 'Trailing zeros never count.' ← FALSE — they count when a decimal point is present.
WRONG: Rounding 4.56 × 1.4 to 4.56 ← you used the sig figs of the larger number, not the smaller.
WRONG: Rounding BEFORE you finish calculating ← always complete the full calculation first.
WATCH OUT: Exact numbers (counted values, defined conversions) do NOT limit your sig fig count.
CORRECT CHECK: Ask — does a decimal point appear? If yes, trailing zeros count. If no, they are ambiguous.
slides.mistake: Thinking 300 and 300.0 have the same sig figs. They do NOT: 300 is ambiguous (1–3), while 300.0 is clearly 4 sig figs because the decimal point is written.

procedureExamples.prompt: How many significant figures are in (a) 0.004500  (b) 20300  (c) 8.010 × 10²?
steps: 0.004500: Leading zeros (0.00) — do NOT count. Digits left: 4, 5, 0, 0. Both trailing zeros follow a decimal point → count. Answer: 4 sig figs.

20300: No decimal point present. Trailing zeros are ambiguous. Non-zero digits plus captive zero: 2, 0 (captive), 3. Trailing zeros → uncertain. Answer: 3 sig figs (assume ambiguous trailing zeros excluded).
8.010 × 10²: Coefficient only. 8 (non-zero), 0 (captive between 8 and 1), 1, 0 (trailing + decimal). Answer: 4 sig figs.

procedureExamples.prompt: Calculate $102.5 - 0.366$ and express in correct sig figs.
steps: Identify decimal places: 102.5 ends at tenths (1 decimal place); 0.366 ends at thousandths (3 decimal places). Fewest decimal places = tenths (102.5).
Round to tenths place → $102.1$

procedureExamples.prompt: Calculate $0.070 \times 430$ and express in correct sig figs.
steps: Count sig figs: 0.070 has 2 sig figs (leading zeros excluded, trailing zero after decimal counts); 430 has 2 sig figs (ambiguous trailing zero excluded).
Multiply: $0.070 \times 430 = 30.1$
Round to 2 sig figs → $30.$  or written as $3.0 \times 10^1$

procedureExamples.prompt: (Group We-Do) A student prepares a saltwater solution: she dissolves a salt sample with a mass of $8.74$ g into a flask and measures the total solution volume as $125$ mL using a graduated cylinder. Calculate the concentration in g/mL and express in correct sig figs.
steps: Sig figs: 45.67 has 4; 5.2 has 2 → answer gets 2 sig figs.
Round to 2 sig figs → $8.8$ g/mL

worksheet.title: Significant Figures — Practice Worksheet
worksheet.instructions: Show all work. Apply sig fig rules to every answer. Use the procedure steps on your notes page if you get stuck.

sections.workedExample:
**Example:** How many sig figs are in $0.003060$?
- Leading zeros (0.00) → do NOT count.
- Remaining digits: 3, 0, 6, 0
- 0 between 3 and 6 = captive zero → counts.
- Trailing 0 after the decimal → counts.
- **Answer: 4 significant figures**
sections.directions: Directions: Count the significant figures in each measurement. Write the number and briefly name the rule for each zero.
problems: How many sig figs are in $52.40$ mL?

🌶 A student reports a mass as $008.050$ g. How many sig figs does this contain, and what is wrong with how it was written?

sections.type: Section 2 — Identifying Sig Figs in Context
sections.workedExample:
**Example:** A thermometer reads $37.0°C$. A different thermometer reads $37°C$. Which is more precise, and how many sig figs does each have?
- $37.0°C$: non-zero digits 3, 7; trailing zero after decimal → counts → **3 sig figs, more precise**.
- $37°C$: only 3 and 7 → **2 sig figs, less precise**.
sections.directions: Directions: Answer each question about sig figs in real measurement context.
problems: A graduated cylinder reads $25.0$ mL. A beaker reads $25$ mL. Which instrument is more precise? How many sig figs does each reading have?
A student writes $1500$ g for a mass. A second student writes $1.500 \times 10^3$ g. Do these represent the same precision? Explain using sig fig counts.
🌶 A recipe calls for exactly $3$ eggs and $1.25$ cups of flour. When calculating the total number of ingredients, which value limits the sig figs of the answer — and why?
A balance measures $0.0560$ kg. Write this in scientific notation and confirm the sig fig count is the same.

sections.type: Section 3 — Sig Figs in Addition and Subtraction
sections.workedExample:
**Example:** $145.67 + 2.3 + 0.025 = ?$
- Step 1: Decimal places — $145.67$: hundredths; $2.3$: **tenths** (fewest); $0.025$: thousandths.
- Step 2: Sum $= 147.995$
- Step 3: Round to tenths → **$148.0$**
sections.directions: Directions: Perform each calculation, then round to the correct number of decimal places.
problems: 🌶 A student measures three lengths: $2.3$ m, $0.446$ m, and $12.0$ m, and needs the total in correct sig figs. She writes $14.746$ m as her final answer. Identify her error and give the correct answer.

sections.type: Section 4 — Sig Figs in Multiplication and Division
sections.workedExample:
**Example:** $3.82 \times 0.030 = ?$
- Step 1: Sig figs — $3.82$: 3 sig figs; $0.030$: **2 sig figs** (leading zeros don't count, trailing zero after decimal does).
- Step 2: Product $= 0.1146$
- Step 3: Round to **2 sig figs** → **$0.11$**
sections.directions: Directions: Perform each calculation, then round to the correct number of significant figures.
problems: A rectangular garden in El Paso measures $12.3$ m by $4.0$ m. What is its area in correct sig figs?
🌶 A student divides $250.0$ mL by $3.0$ min to find a flow rate. She reports $83.33$ mL/min. Identify the error and give the correct answer with units.

procedure: COUNTING: Cross out all leading zeros. Check each remaining zero — captive (between non-zeros) → counts; trailing with decimal → counts; trailing without decimal → ambiguous.
ADD/SUBTRACT: Identify the decimal place (not count) of each number. Round the answer to the FEWEST decimal places among all inputs.
MULTIPLY/DIVIDE: Count sig figs in each number. Round the answer to the FEWEST sig-fig count among all inputs.
Always compute the full mathematical answer BEFORE rounding at the final step.
optionalExtra: **Challenge A:** A scientist in El Paso measures a water sample: $V = 24.5$ mL, $T = 20.°C$, $m = 24.48$ g. Calculate density ($\rho = m/V$) and report it in correct sig figs. Then explain: if the volume had been measured as $24.50$ mL instead, would the answer change? Why or why not?

**Challenge B:** Design-your-own: Write THREE different numbers that each have exactly 4 significant figures — one must contain a captive zero, one a trailing zero with a decimal, and one must be in scientific notation. Then write one 4-sig-fig multiplication problem using two of your numbers and solve it.

exitTicket: How many significant figures are in $0.003060$? Name the rule that makes the final zero significant.
Calculate $8.75 \div 0.50$ and express your answer in the correct number of significant figures.

answers: 1. $52.40$ mL → **4 sig figs**. Non-zero digits 5, 2 count. Trailing zero after decimal (Rule 4) counts. 4 is non-zero, counts.
2. $0.0082$ g → **2 sig figs**. Leading zeros (0.00) are placeholders — Rule 3, do not count. Only 8 and 2 count.
3. $5006$ km → **4 sig figs**. All non-zero digits count (5, 6). The two zeros are captive (between 5 and 6) — Rule 2, both count.
4. $3.000 \times 10^4$ Pa → **4 sig figs**. Only the coefficient matters: 3 (non-zero), then three trailing zeros after the decimal point — Rule 4, all count.

5. 🌶 $008.050$ g → **4 sig figs** (same as $8.050$). The leading zeros (00) are not written in scientific measurements and do not count — Rule 3. The number should be written as $8.050$ g or $8.050$ g; writing extra leading zeros is non-standard and potentially confusing but does not change the sig fig count.
6. $900.$ mL → **3 sig figs**. The decimal point is explicitly written (Rule 4/5), so both trailing zeros count. Digits: 9, 0, 0.

answerKey.section: Section 2 — Identifying Sig Figs in Context
answers: 7. $25.0$ mL (graduated cylinder) → **3 sig figs**, more precise. $25$ mL (beaker) → **2 sig figs**, less precise. More sig figs = more precise instrument.

8. $1500$ g → **2 sig figs** (ambiguous trailing zeros, no decimal). $1.500 \times 10^3$ g → **4 sig figs** (trailing zeros in coefficient after decimal count). They do NOT represent the same precision; scientific notation clarifies.

9. 🌶 The exact number $3$ eggs is counted and has **infinite sig figs** — it does NOT limit the answer. The flour ($1.25$ cups) has **3 sig figs** and is the measured quantity, so it limits the answer. The answer is reported to 3 sig figs.
10. $0.0560$ kg in scientific notation: $5.60 \times 10^{-2}$ kg. Sig fig count: leading zeros removed, digits are 5, 6, 0 (trailing after decimal) → **3 sig figs** — same as original.

answerKey.section: Section 3 — Sig Figs in Addition and Subtraction
answers: 11. $13.5 + 2.45 + 0.007$: $13.5$ ends at tenths (fewest decimal places). Sum $= 15.957$ → round to tenths → **$16.0$**
12. $88.20 - 0.453$: $88.20$ ends at hundredths (fewest). Difference $= 87.747$ → round to hundredths → **$87.75$**
13. $5.0 + 12.001 + 0.35$: $5.0$ ends at tenths (fewest). Sum $= 17.351$ → round to tenths → **$17.4$**

14. 🌶 The student's error: she reported **all digits** without rounding. The fewest decimal places among $2.3$ m (tenths), $0.446$ m (thousandths), $12.0$ m (tenths) is tenths. Correct answer: $14.746$ m → **$14.7$ m**.
15. $1000.0 - 2.45$: $1000.0$ ends at tenths (1 decimal place); $2.45$ ends at hundredths. Fewest = tenths. Difference $= 997.55$ → round to tenths → **$997.6$**

answerKey.section: Section 4 — Sig Figs in Multiplication and Division
answers: 16. $6.21 \times 0.20$: $6.21$ → 3 sf; $0.20$ → **2 sf** (leading zero excluded, trailing zero after decimal counts). Product $= 1.242$ → 2 sf → **$1.2$**

19. 🌶 $250.0 \div 3.0$: $250.0$ → 4 sf; $3.0$ → **2 sf** → answer gets **2 sf**. Quotient $= 83.3\overline{3}$ → round to 2 sf → **$83$ mL/min**. The student's error was reporting 5 sig figs ($83.33$) when 3.0 limits the answer to 2 sig figs.
20. $0.0500 \times 6.70$: $0.0500$ → 3 sf (leading zeros excluded, trailing zeros after decimal count); $6.70$ → 3 sf. Product $= 0.3350$ → 3 sf → **$0.335$**
