vocab.def: the ability to maintain stable internal conditions (like body temperature, water balance, and blood sugar) even when the {{external environment|3cm}} changes; your body does this automatically through {{feedback loops|3cm}}
a response that {{counteracts|2cm}} or reverses a change, pushing the body back toward its {{set point|2cm}}; the main mechanism of homeostasis

examples.label: Concept 1 — How Negative Feedback Maintains Body Temperature
examples.prompt: Explain how your body brings your temperature back to normal when you get cold.
steps: **Step 1—Detect the change:** Temperature sensors in your skin and brain sense that your body is {{below 37°C|3cm}}.
**Step 2—Nervous system responds:** Your brain signals {{muscles|2cm}} to shiver and blood vessels to {{narrow|2cm}}, reducing heat loss.
**Step 3—Temperature rises:** Shivering and reduced heat loss raise your temperature back to {{37°C (your set point)|3cm}}.
**Step 4—Feedback stops:** Once you're warm, the signal stops. Shivering {{slows down|2cm}}, and homeostasis is restored.
examples.answer: Your body detects a temperature drop, responds by shivering and reducing heat loss, temperature rises back to 37°C, then the response stops. This is negative feedback.

examples.label: Concept 2 — Organization: How Cells, Tissues, and Organs Work Together
examples.prompt: Describe the relationship between a muscle cell, muscle tissue, and your arm.
steps: **Step 1—Cells are the building blocks:** {{Muscle cells|2cm}} are the smallest living unit that can contract (shorten).
**Step 2—Tissues are groups of similar cells:** Many muscle cells bundle together to form {{muscle tissue|2cm}}.
**Step 3—Organs are tissues working together:** Muscle tissue, connective tissue, and nerve tissue combine to form a {{muscle (an organ)|2cm}}.
**Step 4—Systems are organs working together:** Your {{muscular system|2cm}} includes all muscles; it works with your {{skeletal system|2cm}} to move your arm.
examples.answer: Muscle cells → muscle tissue → muscles (organs) → muscular system. Each level has a job; each depends on the level below it.

vocab.definition: the ability of your body to maintain stable internal conditions (temperature, water, nutrients, oxygen) even when the outside environment changes
a response that reverses or counteracts a change, pushing your body back toward its normal (set) value

slides.heading: Hook: Your Body's Invisible Act
bullets: Right now, your body is keeping you at 37°C, your blood sugar balanced, your heart pumping, and your oxygen steady—without you thinking about it.
If you jump in a cold pool, your temperature starts to drop. What happens next?
Your brain detects the drop and tells your muscles to shiver. You warm up. Then the shivering stops.
That's **homeostasis**—your body's superpower to stay balanced no matter what happens around you.

slides.heading: What Is Homeostasis?
bullets: **Homeostasis** = the ability to keep internal conditions stable (temperature, water, sugar, oxygen, etc.) even when the outside world changes.
Your body has a **set point** for each condition—the 'normal' value it aims for (body temperature = 37°C, blood glucose ≈ 100 mg/dL).
When something changes, your body **detects it** and **responds** to bring it back to the set point.
This automatic, self-correcting process keeps you alive.

slides.heading: How It Works: Negative Feedback
bullets: **Negative feedback** is the main tool. It means: the response pushes you *back* toward normal, not *away* from it.
Think of a thermostat: if the room gets cold, the heater kicks on. When it's warm enough, the heater turns off. The response cancels out the change.
Your body does the same thing with temperature, sugar, water, and many other things, all day and night.
The key: the response stops once you're back to normal. That keeps you balanced.

slides.heading: Example: Keeping Your Temperature Steady (Cold Day)
bullets: **You get cold:** Temperature drops below 37°C.
**Your body detects it:** Sensors in your skin and brain send a signal.
**Your brain responds:** Tells muscles to shiver; tells blood vessels to narrow (less heat loss).
**You warm up:** Shivering and reduced heat loss raise temperature back to 37°C.
**Response stops:** Once you're warm, shivering slows down. Homeostasis restored.
slides.example: This cycle—detect → respond → return to normal → stop—is **negative feedback**. It works for temperature, blood sugar, water balance, oxygen, and dozens of other things your body keeps steady.
slides.mistake: ❌ **Common mistake:** 'Negative feedback means bad.' NO! Negative means the response *opposes* the change—it's actually the body's repair system.

slides.heading: Organization of Life: Levels That Build Up
bullets: Your body is built in levels, each one depending on the level below:
• **Cells** (the smallest living unit) → build up to → **Tissues** (groups of similar cells doing one job)
• Tissues → build up to → **Organs** (tissues working together—like your heart or brain)
• Organs → build up to → **Organ Systems** (organs working together—like the circulatory system with heart, blood vessels, blood)
• All systems → build up to → **You** (the organism). All levels work together so you stay alive.

slides.heading: You Try (Together)
slides.youTry: Your body temperature drops to 35°C after being outside in winter. Name the system that senses this change and explain what your body does to bring your temperature back up.
bullets: Take 2 minutes with a partner. Write down the system and the response.

**Answer:** The **endocrine system** (specifically the **pancreas**) detects high blood sugar. It releases **insulin**, which tells your cells to take up glucose. Blood sugar drops back to normal (~100 mg/dL). This is negative feedback because the response *opposes* the change (high sugar).

slides.heading: This Week: Homeostasis & Organization
bullets: **Today:** Sign class norms, watch intro video, quick diagnostic to see where we're starting.
**Tomorrow–Thursday:** Dig into each system (digestive, circulatory, nervous, immune, muscular, skeletal, endocrine) and see how homeostasis works in each.
**Friday:** Review and short quiz on the big ideas: homeostasis, negative feedback, and how the systems talk to each other.
By the end of the week, you'll understand how your body keeps itself alive—and why.

procedureExamples.prompt: Your body temperature rises to 38.5°C (fever) because you have an infection. Explain the negative feedback loop that brings your temperature back to normal.
steps: **Detect:** Temperature sensors notice temperature is above the set point (37°C).
**Respond:** Your brain signals blood vessels near the skin to dilate (widen), and you sweat. Heat escapes.
**Return:** Temperature drops back to 37°C.
**Stop:** Once you're at the set point, the signal stops. Sweating slows, blood vessels narrow. Homeostasis restored.
procedureExamples.answer: This is negative feedback: the response (sweating, vasodilation) opposes the change (high temperature) and pushes you back to your set point. The loop stops once you're balanced.

procedureExamples.prompt: A student says, 'My body is made of cells, and that's it. What's this tissue and organ stuff for?' Explain why organization into tissues, organs, and systems matters.
steps: **Cells alone can't survive:** A single muscle cell is too weak to move your arm.
**Tissues multiply the job:** Billions of muscle cells bundle together as muscle tissue. Now they can contract strongly.
**Organs combine skills:** Muscle tissue + nerve tissue + connective tissue = a muscle (an organ). Now it can respond to brain signals and move.
**Systems divide labor:** Your muscular system (all muscles) works with your skeletal system (bones) and nervous system (brain) to move. No system works alone.
procedureExamples.answer: Each level—cells, tissues, organs, systems—does a bigger, more complex job. Organization lets your body do things no single cell could ever do.

worksheet.title: Homeostasis & Organization Diagnostic (Low-Stake Snapshot)
worksheet.instructions: Answer the questions below in as much detail as you can. If you're not sure, write what you think. This is NOT a grade—it helps me see where the class is starting. You can use words, drawings, or numbers.

sections.workedExample: **Example:** 'What is homeostasis?' **Answer:** Homeostasis is when your body keeps conditions like temperature and blood sugar at a steady, balanced level even when your environment changes. Your body does this automatically by detecting changes and responding to bring things back to normal. For example, if you get cold, your muscles shiver to make heat so your temperature goes back to 37°C.

sections.workedExample: **Example:** 'Put these in order from smallest to largest: circulatory system, heart, cardiac muscle cell, blood vessel.' **Answer:** Cardiac muscle cell → blood vessel (and heart muscle tissue) → heart (an organ made of tissue and other structures) → circulatory system (the heart plus all blood vessels, working together).

sections.type: Apply homeostasis to a scenario (interpret & predict)
sections.workedExample: **Example:** 'You run a 5K race. Your body temperature starts to rise. Describe what happens next.' **Answer:** As your temperature rises above 37°C, sensors detect the change. Your brain tells blood vessels near your skin to widen and tells your sweat glands to produce sweat. As sweat evaporates from your skin, heat escapes and your temperature drops back to 37°C. Once you cool down, the sweating slows, and you return to normal. This is negative feedback because your body's response (sweating) opposes the change (high temperature).
sections.directions: Directions: Describe what your body does and why. Use the words 'detect,' 'respond,' 'set point,' and 'negative feedback' if you can.
problems: You haven't eaten in 8 hours, and your blood sugar drops below normal. What system detects this, and what does your body do to bring your blood sugar back up?
🌶 You are very stressed, and your heart rate speeds up to 120 beats per minute. Explain how negative feedback might slow your heart rate back to normal (~70 bpm) once the stress goes away.

procedure: Read each question carefully.
Answer in your own words. You do not need to use a specific format.
If you're unsure, write what you think. Guessing is fine—this helps me see your starting point.
If a question asks you to use a word like 'negative feedback,' try to use it, but it's okay if you don't remember it yet.

exitTicket: Name one body system you learned about today and describe one thing it does to keep you alive.
In one sentence, explain what homeostasis means.

answers: **Homeostasis:** Homeostasis is when your body keeps internal conditions (like temperature and blood sugar) steady and balanced, even when your environment changes. Example: Your body stays at 37°C even on a cold day because your brain tells your muscles to shiver and your blood vessels to narrow, which keeps you warm. This automatic balancing act keeps you alive.

**Negative feedback:** Negative feedback is when your body responds to a change in a way that pushes the condition *back* to normal, not further away. For example, if your temperature rises, sweating cools you down; if your temperature drops, shivering warms you up. It's important for homeostasis because it keeps conditions stable—the response stops once you're back to your set point, so you don't overshoot.

**Body temperature set point:** The set point for body temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). If your temperature drops below 37°C, your body detects the change and responds: muscles shiver, blood vessels narrow, and you feel cold and want to move/exercise to generate heat. These responses warm you back up to 37°C.

**Order from smallest to largest:** Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ System. **Example:** Red blood cell (cell) → Blood tissue (tissue, made of many red cells) → Heart (organ, made of cardiac muscle tissue and other tissues) → Circulatory system (many organs including heart, blood vessels, and blood working together). [Alternate examples acceptable: nerve cell → nerve tissue → brain → nervous system; muscle cell → cardiac muscle tissue → heart → circulatory system.]

**Name a system and list organs:** The **digestive system** includes the mouth, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and liver. It breaks down food into nutrients so your cells can absorb and use them to get energy and build new cells.

answerKey.section: Apply homeostasis to a scenario (interpret & predict)
answers: **Low blood sugar scenario:** The **endocrine system** (specifically the **pancreas**) detects that blood glucose has dropped below ~100 mg/dL. The pancreas responds by releasing **glucagon**, a hormone that travels to the **liver** and tells it to break down stored glycogen into glucose and release it into the blood. Blood glucose rises back to normal. Once glucose is back at the set point, the pancreas stops releasing glucagon. This is **negative feedback** because the response (releasing glucagon and glucose) opposes the change (low blood sugar) and restores balance.

**🌶 Stress and heart rate:** When stress starts, your sympathetic nervous system (part of the nervous system) makes your heart rate jump to 120 bpm to prepare for 'fight or flight.' Once the stress is gone, your **parasympathetic nervous system** takes over and sends signals that slow your heart rate back down to ~70 bpm (your set point). This is **negative feedback**: the response (slowing signals) opposes the change (fast heart rate) and brings you back to resting balance. The higher heart rate was useful during the stress, but once the threat is gone, the nervous system shuts that response off so you don't stay revved up.

**Why 'negative' feedback makes sense:** Negative doesn't mean bad; it means the response *opposes* or goes in the opposite direction from the change. If your temperature goes *up*, the response (sweating) goes *down* the temperature. If blood sugar goes *up*, insulin brings it *down*. The response is 'negative' in the sense that it negates (cancels out or reverses) the change. That's why it keeps you balanced—the response always pushes you back to where you started.

script.title: Directional Terms
script.do: Demonstrate anatomical position: stand at the front of the room, feet together, arms at sides, palms facing forward. Have the class stand and do the same. Then point: 'This way is superior (toward the head). This way is inferior (toward the feet). Anterior is the front of your body. Posterior is the back. Medial is the center. Lateral is the sides.' Use a diagram or the slide; reference the organs shown in worksheet section 3 (heart, liver, stomach).

script.say: Always remember: these directions assume anatomical position. The nose is medial to both ears. The ears are lateral to the nose. The heart is superior to the stomach and anterior to the spine.

Thu.notes:
## Key Idea
Your body is organized in layers, from tiny cells all the way up to you as a whole person. Each level builds on the one before it, and they all work together to keep you alive and healthy.

## Key Terms
- **Cell**: The smallest living unit; all cells come from pre-existing cells.
- **Tissue**: A group of similar cells working together to do one job (muscle, nerve, connective, or epithelial).
- **Organ**: Two or more tissue types joined together to perform a specific function (heart, brain, stomach).
- **Organ system**: A group of organs that work together for a major body function (circulatory, nervous, digestive).
- **Organism**: The complete individual—in this case, you.
- **Homeostasis**: Keeping your internal environment stable (temperature, water, pH) despite outside changes.

## Directional Terms (Anatomical Position)
Imagine standing up straight, arms at your sides, palms facing forward. From that position:
- **Superior** = toward the head; **Inferior** = toward the feet.
- **Anterior** (ventral) = front of the body; **Posterior** (dorsal) = back.
- **Medial** = closer to the midline (center); **Lateral** = away from the midline.
- **Proximal** = closer to the trunk; **Distal** = farther from the trunk (often used for limbs).

## Worked Example
**Prompt**: Trace how the stomach fits into the levels of organization, and identify one directional relationship.

**Steps:**
1. Start at the cell level: The stomach wall is made of smooth muscle cells and epithelial cells (cells).
2. Group similar cells: These cells form smooth muscle tissue and epithelial tissue (tissue).
3. Combine tissue types: The stomach is an organ made of muscle, epithelial, and connective tissues working together (organ).
4. Connect to other organs: The stomach, esophagus, small intestine, and large intestine form the digestive system (organ system).
5. View the whole body: The digestive system is one of many systems in your organism (organism).
6. Directional note: The stomach is **superior** to the small intestine and **anterior** to the kidneys (which sit behind it).

## You Try
Name all five levels in order for the **heart**, and state whether the heart is **superior** or **inferior** to the stomach.

**Your answer:** Cell (cardiac muscle cells) → Tissue (cardiac muscle tissue) → Organ (heart) → Organ system (circulatory system) → Organism (you). The heart is **superior** to the stomach.

examples.prompt: Show how a nerve cell fits into each level of organization.
steps: **Level 1 (Cell):** A single {{nerve cell|2cm}} is the smallest living unit.
**Level 2 (Tissue):** Many nerve cells form {{nerve tissue|2cm}}, which can transmit signals.
**Level 3 (Organ):** Nerve tissue, along with other tissues, makes up the {{brain|1.5cm}}, which is an organ.
**Level 4 (System):** The brain and spinal cord form the {{nervous system|2.5cm}}, which controls the body.

examples.answer: Nerve cell → Nerve tissue → Brain (organ) → Nervous system → You (organism)

examples.label: Homeostasis in Action
examples.prompt: Explain how your body maintains homeostasis when you eat a large, salty meal and your blood becomes too concentrated.
steps: **Problem:** Muscles produce heat during exercise; your body temperature begins to {{rise|2cm}}.
**Response:** Temperature sensors in your {{skin and brain|3cm}} detect the change.
**Action:** Your body {{increases sweating|2.5cm}} and sends more blood to your skin to release heat.
**Result:** Body temperature {{returns to ~37°C|2.5cm}}, and you are back in homeostasis.
examples.answer: Homeostasis maintains a stable internal temperature by triggering cooling responses (sweating, increased blood flow to skin) when you exercise.

**Apply the terms:** The liver is {{superior|2cm}} to the stomach (toward the head) and {{posterior|2cm}} (the liver sits behind the stomach).

youTry.prompt: Name the five levels of organization in order and give a real example for a **muscle cell**.
youTry.answer: **Cell** (muscle cell) → **Tissue** (muscle tissue) → **Organ** (e.g., biceps, heart) → **Organ system** (e.g., muscular system) → **Organism** (you). The muscle cell is the starting building block; many muscle cells make muscle tissue, which is part of an organ, which is part of a system, which is part of your whole body.

youTry.prompt: Your body's blood glucose stays around 100 mg/dL even after eating a candy bar. What is this an example of, and how does your body achieve it?
youTry.answer: This is an example of **homeostasis**. Your body maintains a stable internal temperature despite external changes by sweating, increasing blood flow to the skin, and reducing metabolic heat production—all coordinated by the nervous and circulatory systems.

guidedNotes.summary: The human body is organized in five levels: {{cells|2cm}} → {{tissues|1.5cm}} → {{organs|1.5cm}} → {{organ systems|2.5cm}} → {{organism|1.5cm}}. Each level depends on the one below it. {{Homeostasis|2cm}} keeps your internal environment stable, and {{directional terms|2.5cm}} describe the location of structures relative to anatomical position.

slides.heading: From One Cell to 37 Trillion
bullets: You started as a **single cell**—smaller than the period at the end of this sentence.
That one cell divided again and again, creating trillions of cells organized into tissues, organs, and systems.
Today you are a living, breathing, thinking organism. How did organization make that possible?
**Bell-ringer answer:** As we zoom out from a cell → cells together form tissue → tissues make organs → organs form systems → all systems make you.

slides.heading: The Five Levels of Organization
bullets: **Level 1: Cell** — The smallest living unit (all cells come from pre-existing cells).
**Level 2: Tissue** — Similar cells working together (muscle, nerve, epithelial, connective).
**Level 3: Organ** — Two or more tissues combined for a specific job (heart, brain, stomach).
**Level 4: Organ System** — Organs working together for a major function (circulatory, nervous, digestive).
**Level 5: Organism** — The complete individual—**you**—with all systems cooperating.

slides.heading: Worked Example: The Heart
bullets: **Cell level:** Cardiac muscle cells are specialized to contract.
**Tissue level:** Many cardiac muscle cells + nervous tissue + connective tissue = heart muscle tissue.
**Organ level:** All those tissues work together to form the **heart**, an organ that pumps blood.
**System level:** The heart, blood vessels, and blood form the **circulatory system**.
**Organism level:** The circulatory system delivers oxygen and nutrients to every other system in your body.
slides.example: Cardiac muscle cell → Cardiac muscle tissue → Heart (organ) → Circulatory system → You (organism)

slides.heading: What Is Homeostasis?
bullets: **Definition:** Your body's ability to keep its internal environment stable despite external changes.
**Key conditions:** temperature (~37°C), water balance, pH, glucose level.
**Example — too hot:** Sweat glands release sweat → sweat evaporates → heat is released → temperature drops back to 37°C.
**Example — low glucose:** Pancreas releases glucose into bloodstream → cells absorb it → blood glucose stabilizes.
**Why it matters:** Homeostasis lets your cells work properly. Without it, you cannot survive.

slides.heading: Anatomical Directional Terms
bullets: Always imagine **anatomical position**: standing upright, feet together, arms at sides, palms facing **forward**.
**Superior** = toward the head; **Inferior** = toward the feet.
**Anterior** (front) & **Posterior** (back) — imagine a vertical line running front to back through the center.
**Medial** = closer to center; **Lateral** = away from center.
**Proximal** & **Distal** — used for limbs: proximal = closer to trunk; distal = farther from trunk.

**Your answer:** The right ear is **lateral** to the nose (away from the midline) and slightly **superior** (it sits a bit higher).

slides.heading: This Week's Journey
bullets: **Today:** Levels of organization, homeostasis, and directional terms (this lesson).
**Tomorrow:** Zoom in to **cell structure** — what parts do cells have, and what does each part do?
**Later this week:** The **four tissue types** and how they connect to organs and systems.
**By Friday:** You'll be able to describe how your body stays balanced and organized, from the tiniest cell to your complete self.

procedureExamples.prompt: A student says, 'The stomach is superior to the liver.' Is this correct? Why or why not?
steps: Step 1: Recall the position of both organs. The stomach is in the upper-left abdomen; the liver is a large organ covering much of the upper abdomen and sits partly above the stomach.
Step 2: Determine the relationship. The liver and stomach overlap significantly; the liver is largely **posterior** (behind) and **superior** (above) the stomach.

Step 3: Apply the directional rule. Superior means 'toward the head.' The liver sits higher than the stomach. The statement is **incorrect**; the stomach is **inferior** to the liver, or the liver is **superior** to the stomach.
procedureExamples.answer: The statement is incorrect. The liver is superior to the stomach (the liver sits higher, toward the head).

procedureExamples.prompt: Your friend eats a very sugary snack and their blood glucose spikes to 180 mg/dL. Describe the homeostatic response that brings it back to normal levels.
steps: Step 1: Recognize the problem. Body temperature is below normal (35°C vs. the set point of ~37°C).
Step 2: Identify the response. Temperature sensors in the skin and brain detect the change and trigger the nervous system.
Step 3: Name the action. The body shivers (muscles contract rapidly, generating heat), increases metabolism, and constricts blood vessels in the skin to reduce heat loss.
Step 4: Confirm restoration. Heat production → body temperature returns to 37°C → homeostasis is restored.
procedureExamples.answer: Shivering and increased metabolic heat production raise body temperature back to 37°C, restoring homeostasis.

sections.workedExample:
**Example:** Explain why a single cell cannot do the job of a multicellular organism like you. 
 **Answer:** A single cell is tiny and can only perform a limited number of functions. It cannot simultaneously digest food, pump blood, think, fight infection, and balance temperature. By organizing into tissues (groups of similar cells), organs (tissue teams), and systems (organ teams), your body divides work among specialists—muscle cells focus on contraction, nerve cells focus on signaling, and so on. This division of labor, plus the nervous and endocrine system's ability to coordinate responses, allows homeostasis to maintain stability across all those specialized functions.

answerKey.section: Matching and Labeling — Levels of Organization
answers: **Cell.** A cardiac muscle cell is the smallest living unit and the starting point of organization.
**Tissue.** Nerve tissue is made of many nerve cells working together to transmit signals.
**Organ system.** The nervous system is made of many organs (brain, spinal cord, nerves) working together to control the body.
**Organism.** A complete human being is the highest level, composed of all organ systems.
**Tissue.** Epithelial tissue is a group of epithelial cells that form a lining or covering (in this case, the stomach's inner lining).

**Response:** Sweat glands release sweat onto the skin. As sweat evaporates, it carries heat away from the body. Blood vessels in the skin dilate (widen) to release more heat. Body temperature drops back to 37°C, restoring homeostasis.

**Response:** The kidneys monitor blood water levels. When water is low, the pituitary gland releases a hormone (ADH) that signals the kidneys to reabsorb more water from urine back into the bloodstream. When water is high, less ADH is released, and the kidneys allow more water to be excreted. This keeps blood water and osmolarity in balance—homeostasis maintained.

🌶 **Response:** Without enough insulin, cells cannot efficiently take up glucose from the blood. Blood glucose remains high, causing the cells to be 'starved' for energy despite high blood glucose levels. Over time, high blood glucose damages blood vessels and nerves. The body cannot maintain glucose homeostasis, leading to complications like poor wound healing, nerve damage, and vision problems.

**inferior** (or **caudal**)
**lateral**
**anterior** (or **ventral**)
🌶 **Answer:** The stomach is **inferior** and **anterior** to the liver. (The stomach sits lower/farther from the head than the liver and is positioned in front of/ventral to parts of the liver.)

**Answer:** Different tissues have different specialized functions. When organized into an organ, these tissues work as a team—for example, the heart's muscle tissue contracts, while its nervous tissue coordinates the timing, and connective tissue holds it together. This teamwork produces a function no single tissue could accomplish alone.

**Answer:** (Accept any system with a correct homeostatic mechanism. Example — **Circulatory system:** Delivers oxygen and nutrients to all cells and removes carbon dioxide and waste. This maintains the internal environment (oxygen levels, nutrient availability, waste removal) that cells need to function. Another example — **Nervous system:** Senses internal and external changes and triggers responses (e.g., sweating when hot, shivering when cold) to restore stable temperature and pH.)

🌶 **Answer:** The immune response involves multiple levels: (1) **Cells** — white blood cells (lymphocytes, macrophages) recognize and attack bacteria. (2) **Tissues** — immune tissues like the lymph nodes and bone marrow produce white blood cells. (3) **Organs** — the thymus, spleen, and lymph nodes are lymphoid organs that organize immune cells. (4) **Systems** — the lymphatic and circulatory systems transport immune cells throughout the body to reach the infection site. (5) **Organism** — all these systems coordinate (through chemical signals and neural signals) to mount a whole-body response, fight the infection, and restore homeostasis (normal body temperature, normal white blood cell count, normal healing).

Fri.notes:
## Key Idea
Anatomists use eight **directional terms** to describe where structures are located and how they relate to each other on the human body. These terms create a shared language so that doctors, nurses, and scientists can communicate clearly about anatomy—no matter which way the body is facing or which country they're in.

## Key Terms
- **Anterior:** toward the front of the body
- **Posterior:** toward the back of the body
- **Superior:** toward the head (upper)
- **Inferior:** toward the feet (lower)
- **Medial:** toward the body's center line (the midline that runs down the middle)
- **Lateral:** toward the side, away from the body's center line
- **Proximal:** closer to the trunk (origin point); closer to where a limb attaches
- **Distal:** farther from the trunk; farther from where a limb attaches

## Worked Example: Locating the Liver
**Prompt:** Describe the location of the liver using two directional terms.

**Step 1:** Find the liver on an anatomical diagram. It sits in the upper-right side of the abdomen.

**Step 2:** Ask: Is it above or below the stomach? → It is **superior** (above) the stomach.

**Step 3:** Ask: Is it on the right side or left side of the body? → It is on the right, which is **lateral** to the body's center line (or lateral to the spine).

**Answer:** The liver is superior and lateral (or: superior and to the right).

## You Try
Describe the location of the right knee using two directional terms. Think: Is it above or below the hip? Is it on the midline or to the side?

**Answer:** The right knee is **inferior** (below the hip) and **lateral** (to the right side of the midline, or away from center).

examples.prompt: The liver is located in the upper right abdomen. Compare its position to the small intestine below it. Use 'superior' or 'inferior' to describe the liver's location.
steps: Find the heart and stomach on an anatomical diagram.
Ask: Is the heart higher up (closer to the head) or lower (closer to the feet)?
The heart is higher up, so it is {{superior|2cm}} to the stomach.
Answer: The heart is {{superior|2cm}} to the stomach.
examples.answer: The heart is superior to the stomach (or: above the stomach).

examples.label: Using Medial and Lateral
examples.prompt: You have a bruise on the inside of your left thigh. Is this bruise medial or lateral to your center line?
steps: Imagine a line running down the middle of your body (the {{midline|2cm}}).
Your right arm is on the right side of your body.
The outside of your arm is even farther from the center line.
Since it is away from the center line, it is {{lateral|2cm}}.
examples.answer: The scar is lateral (on the side, away from the center line).

examples.label: Using Proximal and Distal on a Limb
examples.prompt: Your wrist and your fingertips are both on your arm. Which is proximal and which is distal?
steps: Proximal means {{closer to where the limb attaches|3.5cm}} (the shoulder for the arm).
Distal means {{farther from where the limb attaches|3.5cm}}.
Your wrist is closer to your shoulder, so it is {{proximal|2cm}}.
Your fingertips are farther from your shoulder, so they are {{distal|2cm}}.
examples.answer: The wrist is proximal; the fingertips are distal.

youTry.prompt: Your ankle bone is attached to your foot. Is your ankle proximal or distal to your toes?
youTry.answer: Distal. Your knee is farther from where the leg attaches (the hip).

youTry.prompt: You have a bump on your left shoulder. Is that bump medial or lateral? (Hint: think about the center line.)
youTry.answer: Lateral. The right side of the body is away from the center line (midline), so it is lateral.

guidedNotes.summary: The eight directional terms let doctors describe {{where|2cm}} a body structure is and {{how it relates|2.5cm}} to nearby structures. {{Anterior/posterior|2.5cm}}, {{superior/inferior|2.5cm}}, {{medial/lateral|2.5cm}}, and {{proximal/distal|2.5cm}} are opposite pairs that cover all directions on the human body.

Fri.notesExit: Name the directional term that means 'away from the center line of the body' and give one example of a body part that is in that direction.

vocab.definition: Toward the front of the body.
Toward the back of the body.
Toward the head or upper part.
Toward the feet or lower part.
Toward the center line (midline) of the body.
Toward the side; away from the center line.
Closer to the trunk or the point where a limb attaches.
Farther from the trunk or the point where a limb attaches.

slides.heading: Why Directional Terms Matter
bullets: A surgeon reads a patient report: 'Mass found medial to the right knee.'
A physical therapist tells you: 'Your injury is anterior to the hamstring.'
Doctors around the world use the same eight terms to say exactly where something is—no confusion.
Today you'll speak the language of anatomy.

slides.heading: The Eight Directional Terms (Opposite Pairs)
bullets: **Anterior ↔ Posterior:** Front ↔ Back
**Superior ↔ Inferior:** Toward head ↔ Toward feet
**Medial ↔ Lateral:** Toward center line ↔ Away from center line
**Proximal ↔ Distal:** Closer to trunk ↔ Farther from trunk

slides.heading: Body Diagram with Directional Arrows
bullets: Look at the diagram: the dashed line is your **center line** (midline).
Red arrows show **Superior** (up to head) and **Inferior** (down to feet).
Green arrow shows **Medial** (toward center) and **Lateral** (toward side).
Blue arrows show **Proximal** (toward shoulder/trunk) and **Distal** (away from trunk).
slides.graphCaption: Stand up and point to each direction on your own body as we say the terms aloud.

slides.heading: Worked Example: Locating the Lungs
bullets: **The lungs are located in the chest. Describe them using directional terms.**
slides.example:
Step 1: The liver sits in the upper right abdomen → it is **superior** to the small intestine.
Step 2: The liver is on the right side → it is **lateral** to the midline of the body.
Step 3: The liver is closer to the ribs than to the pelvis → the liver is **proximal** to the umbilicus (belly button).

slides.heading: Common Mistake
bullets: ❌ Saying 'medial' when you mean 'middle of the body'—medial means toward the CENTER LINE, not the middle.
❌ Confusing proximal and distal—remember: proximal is closer to where the limb **attaches** (like the shoulder for an arm).
✓ Double-check: Proximal rhymes with 'trunk,' distal rhymes with 'tips.'

slides.heading: We Do: The Elbow
bullets: Your elbow is on your arm. Is it proximal or distal to your wrist?
Think: Your elbow is closer to where your arm attaches (the shoulder).
**Your turn:** Write your answer, then turn to a partner and explain why.
slides.youTry: Is the shoulder proximal or distal to the elbow? Why?

slides.heading: Today & This Week
bullets: **Today:** Learn the eight terms, locate them on a body diagram, practice on worksheets.
**Your job:** Complete Sections 1–3 of the worksheet (about 8 problems).
**What's next:** Label diagrams, compare locations of organs, and use the terms in clinical scenarios.

procedureExamples.prompt: The pancreas is located deep in the abdomen, below the stomach. Describe its position using two directional terms.
steps: Step 1: Is the pancreas above or below the stomach? → It is **inferior** (lower).
Step 2: Is the pancreas in the middle of the abdomen or off to the side? → It is slightly **medial** and posterior (deeper inside), but primarily **inferior to the stomach**.
Answer: The pancreas is **inferior** (and posterior/medial) to the stomach.
procedureExamples.answer: The pancreas is inferior (and posterior) to the stomach.

procedureExamples.prompt: Your index finger and your ring finger are on the same hand. Which is medial and which is lateral?
steps: Step 1: Draw a midline down the center of your hand.
Step 2: Your thumb is on the outside (away from center) → **lateral**.
Step 3: Your little finger is on the inside (toward center) → **medial**.
Answer: The thumb is lateral; the little finger is medial.
procedureExamples.answer: The thumb is lateral; the little finger is medial (toward the center line of the hand).

worksheet.title: Anatomical Directional Terms Practice
worksheet.instructions: Use the eight directional terms (anterior, posterior, superior, inferior, medial, lateral, proximal, distal) to answer each question. You may refer to the body diagram in your guided notes or on the board. Write one or two directional terms for each answer.

sections.type: Identify the direction using a body diagram
sections.workedExample: **Example:** The nose is _____ to the mouth (farther from feet) and _____ to the ears (toward center). **Steps:** (1) Is the nose higher or lower than the mouth? Higher → **superior**. (2) Is the nose in the middle or to the side? Middle → **medial**. **Answer:** The nose is **superior and medial** to the mouth.
sections.directions: Directions: For each pair of structures, write the directional term(s) that describe how the first is positioned relative to the second.
problems: The heart is _____ and _____ to the stomach.
The shoulder is _____ to the elbow.
The brain is _____ to the spinal cord.
The thumb is _____ to the little finger (on the same hand).
🌶 The kneecap is _____ and _____ to the heel (consider height and distance from center line).

sections.type: Describe a location on a limb (proximal vs. distal)
sections.workedExample: **Example:** On your arm, is your elbow proximal or distal to your shoulder? **Steps:** (1) Where does the arm attach to the body? At the shoulder. (2) Is the elbow closer to or farther from that attachment point? Closer. (3) Closer = **proximal**. **Answer:** The elbow is **proximal** to the shoulder.
sections.directions: Directions: Use 'proximal' or 'distal' to complete each sentence.
problems: Your wrist is _____ to your hand.
Your hip is _____ to your knee.
Your ankle is _____ to your toes.
Your forearm is _____ to your shoulder.
🌶 Your knee is _____ to your foot, and your thigh is _____ to your knee. (Use both terms in your answer.)

sections.type: Apply terms to a clinical or everyday scenario
sections.workedExample: **Example:** A doctor tells you that you have inflammation medial to your right knee. Where should you look on your body? **Steps:** (1) 'Medial' means toward the center line. (2) My right knee is on my right side; medial means toward the middle. (3) So the inflammation is on the **inside of the right knee (toward the center of the body)**. **Answer:** You should look on the inside (center-side) of your right knee.
sections.directions: Directions: Read the clinical description and explain where on the body you would find the structure. Use one or more directional terms in your answer.
problems: A nurse examines a patient's anterior arm. Which side of the arm is being examined—the top or the palm side?
A physical therapist says, 'The injury is distal to your hip.' Is the injury closer to your foot or closer to your trunk?
🌶 A radiologist reports: 'There is a small bone fragment superior and posterior to the right elbow.' Describe in your own words where this fragment is located.

procedure: 1. Identify the two body structures mentioned (e.g., heart and stomach).
2. Visualize their positions on your body or on the diagram.

3. Ask: 'Which structure is higher (superior) or lower (inferior)? Which is toward the center line (medial) or toward the side (lateral)? Which is closer to (proximal) or farther from (distal) the attachment point?'
4. Write the directional term(s) that answer your question.
optionalExtra: 🌶 Challenge: A surgeon says, 'We will make an incision anterior to the left ear, superior to the jaw line, and medial to the temple.' Sketch a simple head from the front, and mark with an 'X' where you think this incision will be. Explain your answer using all three directional terms.

extension.title: Challenge
extension.prompt: A surgeon says, 'We will make an incision anterior to the left ear, superior to the jaw line, and medial to the temple.' Sketch a simple head from the front, and mark with an 'X' where you think this incision will be. Explain your answer using all three directional terms.
extension.why: This challenge requires you to synthesize all three directional terms at once and visualize a real anatomical scenario. It moves beyond labeling single pairs and asks you to locate a precise point using multiple directional references—a skill surgeons use every day.

exitTicket: In one sentence, explain what the word 'distal' means and give an example of a body part that is distal to another.

answerKey.section: Identify the direction using a body diagram
answers: **Superior and anterior** (or posterior—the heart is behind the front of the rib cage, but primarily superior to the stomach).
**Proximal** (the shoulder is closer to where the arm attaches to the trunk).
**Superior and posterior** (the brain is above and behind the spinal cord).
**Lateral** (the thumb is on the side, away from the center line; the little finger is medial).

**Inferior and lateral** (the kneecap is lower than the heel and farther from the center line, as it sits on the outer surface of the leg). _Challenge note: Some sources also accept 'inferior' alone if the focus is on the height difference; 'lateral' captures the side position clearly._

answerKey.section: Describe a location on a limb (proximal vs. distal)
answers: **Proximal** (the wrist is closer to the shoulder, where the arm attaches).
**Proximal** (the hip is closer to where the leg attaches).
**Distal** (the ankle is farther from where the leg attaches).
**Distal** (the forearm is farther from the shoulder attachment).
**Proximal** and **Distal**: Your knee is proximal to your foot (closer to the attachment at the hip), and your thigh is proximal to your knee (the thigh is even closer to the hip attachment).

answerKey.section: Apply terms to a clinical or everyday scenario
answers: The **anterior arm** is the palm side (the side facing forward when you stand with your arms at your sides; this is the underside if your arms are relaxed).
The injury is closer to your **foot** (distal = farther from the attachment point; the farther you go from the hip, the closer you get to the foot).

The bone fragment is located **above and behind the right elbow**. It is higher up (toward the head) and on the back side of the arm. It would be felt or seen on the back/upper surface of the right elbow area.

Mon.notes:
## Key Idea
Anatomy and physiology are two linked sciences that together explain how the human body is **built** and how it **works**. Scientists organize the body into levels — from the tiniest chemical building blocks all the way up to the whole organism — and they use a shared vocabulary to describe exactly where body parts are located.

---

## Key Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Anatomy** | The study of the **structure** of the body (what it looks like and how parts are arranged) |
| **Physiology** | The study of the **function** of the body (how parts work) |
| **Anatomical position** | The standard reference pose: body upright, feet together, palms facing forward |
| **Superior** | Toward the head / upper part of the body |
| **Inferior** | Toward the feet / lower part of the body |
| **Anterior (ventral)** | Toward the front of the body |
| **Posterior (dorsal)** | Toward the back of the body |
| **Medial** | Toward the midline (center) of the body |
| **Lateral** | Away from the midline, toward the side |

---

## Levels of Structural Organization (Smallest → Largest)

**Step 1 — Chemical level:** Atoms bond to form molecules (e.g., water, DNA).

**Step 2 — Cellular level:** Molecules combine to form **cells** — the basic unit of life (e.g., a muscle cell).

**Step 3 — Tissue level:** Similar cells working together form a **tissue** (e.g., muscle tissue).

**Step 4 — Organ level:** Two or more tissue types together form an **organ** (e.g., the heart).

**Step 5 — Organ system level:** Related organs working together form an **organ system** (e.g., the cardiovascular system).

**Step 6 — Organism level:** All organ systems together make one living **organism** (you!).

> Memory trick: **C**heerful **C**ats **T**ake **O**n **O**dd **O**rdeals — Chemical, Cellular, Tissue, Organ, Organ system, Organism.

---

## You Try

1. Is the study of how the lungs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide an example of **anatomy** or **physiology**? Explain in one sentence.
2. Place these in order from smallest to largest: *organ system, tissue, cell, organ, organism, chemical*.
3. The navel (belly button) is __________ to the chin and __________ to the knee. (Choose: superior / inferior.)

*(Answers: 1. Physiology — it focuses on function/process. 2. Chemical → Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism. 3. Inferior to the chin; superior to the knee.)*

vocab.def: The study of the {{structure|2.5cm}} of the body — what body parts look like and how they are arranged.
The study of the {{function|2.5cm}} of the body — how body parts work and carry out life processes.
A standard reference pose: body {{upright|2cm}}, feet together, arms at sides, palms facing {{forward|2cm}}.
Describes a structure that is closer to the {{midline|2cm}} (center) of the body than another structure.
Describes a structure that is farther from the {{midline|2cm}}, toward the {{side|1.5cm}} of the body.

examples.label: Concept 1 — Anatomy vs. Physiology
examples.prompt: How do anatomy and physiology differ, and how do they connect?
steps: Anatomy focuses on {{structure|2.5cm}} — the shape, size, and arrangement of body parts.
Physiology focuses on {{function|2.5cm}} — the processes and how parts carry out life activities.
Example: A cardiologist studies heart {{anatomy|2cm}} when looking at valve shape, but heart {{physiology|2cm}} when measuring pumping rate.
The two fields are connected because {{structure determines function|4cm}} — the shape of a part reflects what it does.
examples.answer: Anatomy = structure; Physiology = function; structure always determines function.

examples.label: Concept 2 — Levels of Structural Organization
examples.prompt: Arrange the levels from smallest to largest and give one example for each.
steps: Level 1 (smallest): {{Chemical|2cm}} — atoms and molecules (e.g., water, glucose).
Level 2: {{Cellular|2cm}} — the basic unit of life (e.g., a red blood cell).
Level 3: {{Tissue|2cm}} — groups of similar cells (e.g., cardiac muscle tissue).
Level 4: {{Organ|2cm}} — two or more tissue types (e.g., the heart).
Level 5: {{Organ system|2.5cm}} — related organs working together (e.g., cardiovascular system).
Level 6 (largest): {{Organism|2cm}} — all systems together make one living individual.
examples.answer: Chemical → Cellular → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism

examples.label: Concept 3 — Directional Terminology
examples.prompt: Use directional terms to describe the relationship between two body structures.
steps: Always assume the body is in {{anatomical position|3cm}} before applying any directional term.
The nose is {{superior|2cm}} to the mouth because the nose is closer to the head.
The spine is {{posterior|2cm}} to the stomach because the spine is toward the back.
The sternum (breastbone) is {{medial|2cm}} to the ribs because it runs along the body's centerline.

vocab.definition: The scientific study of the structure of the body and the relationships among its parts.
The scientific study of how the body and its parts function.
The smallest level of organization; includes atoms and the molecules they form (e.g., water, proteins).
The level at which atoms and molecules form cells — the basic structural and functional units of life.
Groups of similar cells that work together to perform a specific function (e.g., muscle tissue, nervous tissue).
Two or more tissue types that together perform specific body functions (e.g., the heart, the kidney).
A group of related organs that work together to accomplish a major body function (e.g., the digestive system).
The highest level — all organ systems functioning together as one living individual.
The standard reference body position: standing upright, feet together, arms at the sides, palms facing forward.
Toward the head or upper part of the body.
Toward the feet or lower part of the body.
Toward the front of the body.
Toward the back of the body.
Toward the midline (center) of the body.
Away from the midline, toward the side of the body.

presentation.title: Anatomy & Physiology — Day 1: Organization and Terminology

slides.heading: 37 Trillion Cells — One Body. How?
bullets: Right now, your body contains roughly 37 TRILLION living cells.
Each cell has a job — and they all coordinate without you thinking about it.
Science needs a system to organize, name, and describe all of this.
Today: you'll learn THAT system — the vocabulary scientists use every single day.
By the end of class, you can define anatomy & physiology, name 6 levels of organization, and say exactly WHERE something is on the body.

slides.heading: Two Sciences, One Body
bullets: ANATOMY: the study of body STRUCTURE — what parts look like and how they are arranged.
PHYSIOLOGY: the study of body FUNCTION — how parts work and why.
These two are always linked: STRUCTURE determines FUNCTION.
Example — Anatomy: 'The heart has four chambers.' Physiology: 'The heart pumps blood by contracting.'
El Paso connection: ER nurses at UMC use both — they LOOK at a broken bone (anatomy) and assess how it affects movement (physiology).

vocab.definition: Study of body structure — what it looks like and how parts are arranged.
Study of body function — how parts work and carry out life processes.

slides.heading: 6 Levels of Structural Organization
bullets: Scientists organize the body from smallest to largest — 6 levels total.
Each level BUILDS on the one below it.
Memory trick: Cheerful Cats Take On Odd Ordeals (Chemical → Cellular → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism).
Chemical: atoms and molecules | Cellular: basic unit of life
Tissue: similar cells grouped | Organ: 2+ tissue types | Organ system: related organs | Organism: the whole you
slides.graphCaption: Levels pyramid — smallest (chemical) at top, largest (organism) at base.

slides.heading: Worked Example — Identifying Levels
bullets: Question: Cardiac (heart) muscle cells group together to form cardiac muscle — what level is that?
Step 1: Identify what is being described — a group of SIMILAR cells working together.
Step 2: Match to a level — groups of similar cells = TISSUE level.
Answer: Cardiac muscle is at the TISSUE level.
Follow-up: When those tissues combine with connective tissue and nerve tissue to form the heart — that becomes the ORGAN level.
slides.example:
1. Similar cells grouped → TISSUE level
2. Two or more tissues forming one structure → ORGAN level
3. Heart + blood vessels working together → ORGAN SYSTEM level

slides.heading: Anatomical Terminology — Everyone Speaks the Same Language
bullets: ANATOMICAL POSITION: upright body, feet together, arms at sides, palms facing FORWARD — the universal reference.
Why? Without a standard pose, 'left' and 'right' would mean something different depending on how you're standing.
SUPERIOR = toward the head | INFERIOR = toward the feet
ANTERIOR (ventral) = toward the front | POSTERIOR (dorsal) = toward the back
MEDIAL = toward the midline (center) | LATERAL = toward the side

vocab.definition: Standing upright, feet together, palms facing forward — the reference pose for ALL directional terms.
Toward the head.
Toward the feet.
Toward the midline.
Toward the side.

slides.heading: Body Direction Reference Diagram
bullets: The body is in anatomical position: upright, palms forward.
SUPERIOR (head end) is UP on the diagram; INFERIOR (foot end) is DOWN.
ANTERIOR = front surface | POSTERIOR = back surface.
The dashed center line = the MIDLINE. Structures closer to it are MEDIAL; farther away are LATERAL.
Use these terms ALWAYS — never say 'up/down/front/back' in a science context.

procedureExamples.prompt: A doctor says the appendix is at the 'cellular level' of organization. Is the doctor correct? Explain why or why not.
steps: Step 1: Recall the 6 levels — Chemical, Cellular, Tissue, Organ, Organ system, Organism.
Step 2: Identify what the appendix IS — it is a structure made of multiple tissue types (epithelial, muscle, connective) working together.
Step 3: Match to the correct level — a structure built from 2+ tissues = ORGAN level.
Step 4: Conclude — the doctor is INCORRECT. The appendix is at the ORGAN level, not the cellular level.
procedureExamples.answer: Incorrect — the appendix is at the ORGAN level (2+ tissue types forming one structure).

procedureExamples.prompt: Describe the location of the sternum (breastbone) relative to TWO other structures using correct directional terms.
steps: Step 1: Assume anatomical position (body upright, palms forward).
Step 2: Compare sternum to the spine — the spine is POSTERIOR (toward the back), so the sternum is ANTERIOR to the spine.
Step 3: Compare sternum to the left shoulder — the shoulder is LATERAL (away from the midline), so the sternum is MEDIAL to the left shoulder.
Step 4: Write the answer in complete, precise language.
procedureExamples.answer: The sternum is ANTERIOR to the spine and MEDIAL to the left shoulder.

procedureExamples.prompt: A lab report says: 'The sample was taken from the superior, medial region of the right arm.' Describe in plain language where this sample came from.
steps: Step 1: Inferior = toward the foot end of the body → lower leg.
Step 2: Lateral = toward the side, away from the midline → outer side of the leg.
Step 3: Combine: the sample came from the OUTER, LOWER part of the left leg — roughly the outer calf/ankle area.
procedureExamples.answer: The outer, lower portion of the left leg — approximately the outer calf or ankle region.

procedureExamples.prompt: Classify each example as anatomy, physiology, or both: (a) Counting the number of bones in the hand. (b) Measuring how fast nerve signals travel. (c) Noting that the heart has four chambers that contract in sequence.
steps: Step 1: Anatomy = structure; Physiology = function.
(a) Counting bones → describes structure/arrangement → ANATOMY.
(b) Speed of nerve signals → a process/function → PHYSIOLOGY.
(c) Four chambers (structure) + contracting in sequence (function) → BOTH anatomy and physiology.
procedureExamples.answer: (a) Anatomy (b) Physiology (c) Both

worksheet.title: Unit 1 Day 1 Practice — Organization & Anatomical Terminology
worksheet.instructions: Use your guided notes and word bank to complete each section. Write all answers in complete words or sentences where indicated. Assume anatomical position for all directional term questions.

sections.type: Section 1 — Anatomy vs. Physiology: Classify the Statement
sections.workedExample:
**Example:** 'The femur (thigh bone) is the longest bone in the human body.' → This describes STRUCTURE (what the femur looks like/its size) → **Anatomy**. 
*Ask yourself: Is it describing WHAT something looks like (anatomy) or HOW something works (physiology)?*
sections.directions: Directions: Write ANATOMY, PHYSIOLOGY, or BOTH to classify each statement. If you write BOTH, underline the part that refers to structure and circle the part that refers to function.
problems: The small intestine is about 6 meters long and is coiled inside the abdominal cavity.
The lungs absorb oxygen from the air and release carbon dioxide into the air with each breath.
The stomach has thick muscular walls that churn food into a semi-liquid mixture.

🌶 A textbook chapter describes how the biceps muscle is attached to the radius bone by a tendon, and explains that this arrangement allows the muscle to flex the forearm at the elbow. Classify the chapter as anatomy, physiology, or both — and quote the specific phrase that justifies each classification.
The skin acts as a barrier that prevents pathogens (germs) from entering the body.
The kidneys are bean-shaped organs located on either side of the spine.

sections.type: Section 2 — Levels of Structural Organization: Match and Order
sections.workedExample:
**Example:** 'A group of smooth muscle cells that line the wall of the stomach.' → Multiple SIMILAR cells working together to perform a function → **Tissue level**. 
*Tip: Chemical = atoms/molecules | Cell = basic unit of life | Tissue = similar cells grouped | Organ = 2+ tissues | Organ system = related organs | Organism = whole individual.*
sections.directions: Directions: Identify the level of structural organization (Chemical, Cellular, Tissue, Organ, Organ system, or Organism) for each description.
problems: A single white blood cell defending the body against infection.
The digestive system — including the mouth, esophagus, stomach, intestines, and liver — all working together to break down food.
DNA molecules inside the nucleus of a cell.

🌶 A scientist is studying a structure that contains epithelial tissue, connective tissue, and smooth muscle tissue working together — and this structure connects to other similar structures to form the urinary system. Name the LEVEL of the structure described AND the level of the complete urinary system. Explain how you know.
The entire human body of a student sitting in science class.
The liver — an organ made of hepatic cells, blood vessels, connective tissue, and bile ducts.

sections.type: Section 3 — Directional Terminology: Choose the Correct Term
sections.workedExample: **Example:** 'The nose is __________ to the chin.' → The nose is CLOSER to the head (top of the body) than the chin is. Closer to the head = **superior**. → Answer: The nose is **superior** to the chin.
sections.directions: Directions: Fill in the blank with the correct directional term. Choose from: superior, inferior, anterior, posterior, medial, lateral.
problems: The forehead is __________ to the chin.
The belly button is __________ to the spine (back of the body).
The pinky finger is __________ to the thumb.
The ears are __________ to the nose.
The toes are __________ to the knee.
The kneecap (patella) is on the __________ surface of the knee.

sections.workedExample: **Example:** 'A nurse says the patient has pain in the superior, medial region of the right arm.' → Superior = toward the head (upper arm area). Medial = toward the midline (inner side). → The pain is in the **upper, inner part of the right arm** — roughly the armpit region.
sections.directions: Directions: Read each scenario and answer in one or two complete sentences using correct anatomical terms.
problems: A medical report states the injury is to the 'inferior, lateral region of the left leg.' Describe in plain language where this injury is located.
🌶 A student claims: 'Studying how scar tissue forms after a cut is ONLY physiology — not anatomy.' Do you agree or disagree? Use the definitions of anatomy and physiology to support your answer.
A biologist is examining a sample under a microscope and sees a single, complete living unit with a nucleus and cell membrane. At what level of organization is this sample, and how do you know?

procedure: Step 1 — Read the statement or scenario carefully.
Step 2 — Identify the key clue: Is it describing STRUCTURE or FUNCTION? A single unit or a group? Location relative to head/feet/center/side?
Step 3 — Match your clue to the correct term or level using your word bank.
Step 4 — Write your answer and check: does it make sense in anatomical position?
optionalExtra: Challenge A — Design-Your-Own: Create TWO original statements about the human body — one that is purely anatomy, and one that is purely physiology. Then write a THIRD statement that is BOTH, and underline the anatomy part and circle the physiology part. Use a real body structure you haven't seen on this worksheet.

Challenge B — You are a medical illustrator. Using the body outline below (sketch a simple stick figure in anatomical position), label at least SIX directional terms with arrows pointing to the correct region. Then write a sentence for each label explaining why that term applies to that region. [Students draw their own outline in this space.]

extension.title: Challenge — Body as a System of Systems
extension.prompt: A physiologist says: 'You cannot fully understand the function of any organ without understanding the organ SYSTEM it belongs to.' Do you agree or disagree? Choose ONE organ system (not the digestive or cardiovascular — use a system you haven't discussed today). Identify at least TWO organs in that system, state what level of organization each organ represents, and explain in 3-4 sentences how removing ONE of those organs would affect the function of the ENTIRE system. Use at least four directional terms to describe the locations of the organs you chose.
extension.why: Extends the levels-of-organization skill by requiring students to apply both structural hierarchy (organ → organ system) and directional terminology simultaneously in a novel organ system context not modeled in class — while also constructing a systems-thinking argument about structure-function relationships.

exitTicket: In ONE sentence, explain the difference between anatomy and physiology. Give a specific example of each.
List the six levels of structural organization in order from smallest to largest: _____ → _____ → _____ → _____ → _____ → _____.

answerKey.procedure: Ask: Does the statement describe WHAT something looks like or IS (anatomy) or HOW something works/what it does (physiology)? If both structure AND function appear, classify as BOTH.
answers: 1. ANATOMY — describes the length and location (structure) of the small intestine. No function is mentioned.
2. PHYSIOLOGY — describes the PROCESS of gas exchange (what the lungs do, not what they look like).

3. BOTH — 'thick muscular walls' = anatomy (structure); 'churn food into a semi-liquid mixture' = physiology (function). Underline 'thick muscular walls'; circle 'churn food into a semi-liquid mixture'.

4. 🌶 BOTH. Anatomy phrase: 'attached to the radius bone by a tendon' — describes the physical arrangement/connection of structures. Physiology phrase: 'allows the muscle to flex the forearm at the elbow' — describes the functional result of that arrangement. Both aspects are present and the student must quote each.
5. PHYSIOLOGY — 'acts as a barrier that prevents pathogens from entering' describes a function/process the skin performs.
6. ANATOMY — 'bean-shaped' and 'located on either side of the spine' describe the structure and position of the kidneys.

answerKey.procedure: Match the description to the level: Chemical = atoms/molecules; Cellular = single cell; Tissue = similar cells grouped; Organ = 2+ tissue types; Organ system = related organs; Organism = whole individual.
answers: 7. CELLULAR level — a single white blood cell is one complete cell, the basic unit of life.
8. ORGAN SYSTEM level — multiple related organs (mouth, esophagus, stomach, intestines, liver) working together = organ system (digestive system).
9. CHEMICAL level — DNA is a molecule; molecules are at the chemical level of organization.

10. 🌶 The structure described (containing epithelial, connective, and smooth muscle tissue) is at the ORGAN level — it is built from multiple (2+) tissue types working together as one functional unit. The complete urinary system is at the ORGAN SYSTEM level — multiple related organs working together. Evidence: the organ level is defined by 2+ tissue types; the organ system level is defined by related organs functioning together.
11. ORGANISM level — the entire human body (all organ systems functioning together) = one living organism.
12. ORGAN level — the liver is a single structure composed of multiple tissue types (hepatic cells, blood vessels, connective tissue, bile ducts).

answerKey.procedure: Assume anatomical position. Determine the correct axis (head-foot = superior/inferior; front-back = anterior/posterior; center-side = medial/lateral) and then choose the correct pole.
answers: 13. SUPERIOR — the forehead is closer to the head (top) than the chin.
14. ANTERIOR — the belly button is on the front surface of the body; the spine is on the back (posterior) surface, so the belly button is anterior to the spine.
15. LATERAL — the pinky finger is farther from the midline than the thumb; the thumb is medial.
16. LATERAL — the ears are farther from the midline (center of the face) than the nose.
17. INFERIOR — the toes are farther toward the feet (lower) than the knee.
18. ANTERIOR — the kneecap sits on the FRONT surface of the knee, which is the anterior surface.

answerKey.procedure: Translate anatomical directional terms into plain-language location descriptions, OR apply definitions to evaluate a claim.
answers: 19. Inferior = toward the feet (lower leg). Lateral = toward the side, away from the midline (outer side of the leg). The injury is located on the OUTER, LOWER portion of the left leg — approximately the outer calf or outer ankle region.

20. 🌶 Disagree. Scar tissue formation involves BOTH anatomy AND physiology. Anatomy: the scar has a specific structure — dense irregular connective tissue that is different in composition and arrangement from the original skin layers. Physiology: the process of scar formation (fibroblast migration, collagen deposition, wound contraction) is a functional/process description. Therefore, studying scar formation involves examining both the structure of the scar (anatomy) and the processes by which it forms (physiology).

21. CELLULAR level — a single, complete living unit with a nucleus and a cell membrane is, by definition, ONE CELL. The cellular level is the level of the individual cell — the basic structural and functional unit of life.

answerKey.procedure: Student-generated examples — award full credit if: the anatomy example describes structure/arrangement ONLY; the physiology example describes function/process ONLY; the BOTH example clearly contains a structural phrase and a functional phrase, each correctly identified.
answers: Challenge A: Exemplary response — Anatomy: 'The human tibia (shin bone) has a triangular cross-section and is the second-largest bone in the body.' (structure only) | Physiology: 'The pancreas secretes insulin in response to rising blood glucose levels.' (process/function only) | Both: 'The bicuspid valve, located between the left atrium and left ventricle [anatomy], prevents the backflow of blood during ventricular contraction [physiology].' Accept any well-formed student-generated example following these rules.

answerKey.procedure: Assess the body outline diagram for: (1) figure drawn in anatomical position (upright, palms forward), (2) at least 6 directional term labels with arrows pointing to a correct body region, (3) a sentence for each label explaining why the term applies. Award full credit for accuracy of labels and quality of justification.
answers: Challenge B: Accept any diagram where the figure is in anatomical position and labels are anatomically correct. Example labels with justifications: SUPERIOR arrow → head region: 'Superior describes regions toward the head — the skull is the most superior part of the body.' | INFERIOR arrow → feet: 'Inferior describes regions toward the feet — the toes are the most inferior structures.' | ANTERIOR arrow → front of torso: 'Anterior means toward the front surface — the chest and abdomen face anteriorly.' | POSTERIOR arrow → back: 'Posterior means toward the back — the spine and shoulder blades are on the posterior surface.' | MEDIAL arrow → center of chest/sternum: 'Medial means toward the midline — the sternum runs along the body's center.' | LATERAL arrow → outer arm: 'Lateral means away from the midline — the outer upper arm is lateral to the chest.' Award bonus credit for any additional correct labels (e.g., proximal/distal on a limb if student knows those terms).

Tue.notes:
## Key Idea
Directional terms describe WHERE one body structure is located **relative to another**. They always assume the body is in **anatomical position** (standing upright, feet forward, palms facing forward).

## Key Terms
| Term | Meaning | Opposite |
|---|---|---|
| **Superior** | toward the head | Inferior |
| **Inferior** | toward the feet | Superior |
| **Anterior** | toward the front of the body | Posterior |
| **Posterior** | toward the back of the body | Anterior |
| **Medial** | toward the midline of the body | Lateral |
| **Lateral** | away from the midline | Medial |
| **Proximal** | closer to the point of attachment/origin | Distal |
| **Distal** | farther from the point of attachment/origin | Proximal |
| **Superficial** | closer to the body surface | Deep |
| **Deep** | farther from the body surface | Superficial |

## How to Apply a Directional Term — Step by Step
**Step 1:** Identify the TWO structures being compared.
**Step 2:** Choose the correct axis (head-to-foot? front-to-back? midline? limb attachment? surface?).
**Step 3:** Decide which structure fits the 'closer to / farther from' rule for that axis.
**Step 4:** Write the sentence: 'Structure A is [term] to Structure B.'

**Worked Example:** Is the knee superior or inferior to the hip?
- Step 1: Structures = knee and hip.
- Step 2: Axis = head-to-foot (superior/inferior).
- Step 3: Hip is closer to the head; knee is farther from the head.
- Step 4: **The knee is inferior to the hip.**

## You Try
Describe the relationship between the elbow and the wrist using a proximal/distal term. Write a complete sentence.
*(Answer: The elbow is proximal to the wrist — the elbow is closer to the shoulder, the point of attachment for the arm.)*

vocab.def: The body standing {{upright|2cm}}, arms at the sides, palms facing {{forward|2cm}} — used as the universal reference for all directional descriptions.
Words that describe the {{location|2cm}} of one body structure relative to {{another|2cm}}; always relative, never absolute.
An imaginary {{vertical|2cm}} line dividing the body into equal left and right halves; medial means toward this line, lateral means {{away|2cm}} from it.

examples.label: Concept 1 — Applying Superior / Inferior
examples.prompt: Is the chin superior or inferior to the forehead?
steps: Identify the two structures: chin and {{forehead|2cm}}.
This pair uses the {{head-to-foot|3cm}} axis, so we choose superior or inferior.
The forehead is closer to the top of the head, so the chin is {{inferior|2cm}} to the forehead.
Full sentence: 'The chin is inferior to the {{forehead|2.5cm}}.'
examples.answer: The chin is inferior to the forehead.

examples.label: Concept 2 — Applying Proximal / Distal on a Limb
examples.prompt: Is the knee proximal or distal to the ankle?
steps: Identify structures: knee and {{ankle|2cm}}.
Proximal/distal applies to {{limbs|2cm}} — measured from the point of {{attachment|2.5cm}} to the trunk.
The knee is {{closer|1.5cm}} to the hip (attachment point) than the ankle is.
Answer: The knee is {{proximal|2cm}} to the ankle.
examples.answer: The knee is proximal to the ankle.

examples.label: Concept 3 — Medial vs. Lateral
examples.prompt: Compare the position of the belly button (navel) and the hip using medial/lateral. Which is medial, and which is lateral?
steps: The midline runs down the {{center|2cm}} of the face.
The nose sits ON the midline — it is {{medial|2cm}} to the ear.
The ear is farther from the midline — it is {{lateral|2cm}} to the nose.
Both statements describe the same relationship from {{opposite|2cm}} perspectives.
examples.answer: The nose is medial to the ear; the ear is lateral to the nose.

youTry.prompt: Use a directional term to complete: 'The shoulder is _______ to the elbow.'
youTry.answer: Proximal — the shoulder is closer to the trunk (point of attachment for the arm) than the elbow is.

youTry.prompt: A patient reports pain on the front of their thigh. Is this pain located on the anterior or posterior surface of the body?
youTry.answer: Posterior — the back faces away from the front of the body, which is the posterior surface.

presentation.title: Directional Terms: Speaking the Language of Anatomy

slides.heading: Would You Know Where to Operate?
bullets: A surgeon's note reads: 'Incision 3 cm superior to the umbilicus, slightly lateral to the midline.'
If you don't know anatomical directional terms, you can't safely understand OR give medical instructions.
Today's goal: use 5 term pairs to describe EXACTLY where any structure is on the body.
All directions assume ANATOMICAL POSITION — standing, palms forward. That never changes.

slides.heading: The 5 Directional Term Pairs — Your Toolkit
bullets: SUPERIOR ↔ INFERIOR — head end vs. foot end
ANTERIOR ↔ POSTERIOR — front of body vs. back of body
MEDIAL ↔ LATERAL — toward midline vs. away from midline
PROXIMAL ↔ DISTAL — closer to trunk attachment vs. farther from it (used on limbs)
SUPERFICIAL ↔ DEEP — near the surface vs. far from the surface

vocab.definition: Toward the head
Toward the feet
Toward the front
Toward the back
Toward the midline
Away from the midline
Closer to attachment point
Farther from attachment point
Near the body surface
Far from the body surface

slides.heading: Reference: Body in Anatomical Position
bullets: Anatomical position is ALWAYS the starting point — no exceptions.
Superior = toward the head | Inferior = toward the feet
Anterior = front of body | Posterior = back of body
Midline divides left from right — medial is toward it, lateral is away from it
On limbs: proximal = closer to where it attaches to the trunk
slides.graphCaption: Labeled body in anatomical position showing all five directional term axes

slides.heading: I-Do: Applying Directional Terms Step by Step
bullets: Question: Is the sternum (breastbone) medial or lateral to the shoulder?
Step 1 — Identify the two structures: sternum and shoulder.
Step 2 — Choose the axis: we are comparing distance from the midline → use MEDIAL/LATERAL.
Step 3 — The sternum is ON the midline of the chest; the shoulder is far from it.
Step 4 — Answer: The sternum is MEDIAL to the shoulder.
slides.example:
1. Structures: sternum vs. shoulder
2. Axis: midline → medial/lateral
3. Sternum = at midline; shoulder = away from midline
4. The sternum is MEDIAL to the shoulder.

slides.heading: Watch Out: The Most Common Mix-Up
bullets: ❌ Students often confuse PROXIMAL/DISTAL with SUPERIOR/INFERIOR — they are NOT the same!
Superior/Inferior → used for the whole body along the head-to-foot axis.
Proximal/Distal → used ONLY when describing position along a LIMB (arm or leg), relative to where it attaches.
✅ Example: The knee is INFERIOR to the hip (whole-body) AND PROXIMAL to the ankle (on the leg limb).
Tip: If you're on a limb, think 'closer to the trunk = proximal.'
slides.mistake: Using proximal/distal for whole-body comparisons (e.g., 'the head is proximal to the feet') — WRONG; use superior/inferior instead.

slides.heading: We-Do #1: Group Practice — Choose the Term
bullets: With your table group, pick the best directional term for each:
A) The heart is _______ to the stomach. (superior / inferior)
B) The skin is _______ to the muscle beneath it. (superficial / deep)
C) The pinky toe is _______ to the big toe. (medial / lateral)
D) The elbow is _______ to the wrist. (proximal / distal)
Discuss — be ready to explain your reasoning, not just your answer.
slides.youTry: A) superior  B) superficial  C) lateral  D) proximal

slides.heading: We-Do #2: Write a Complete Sentence
bullets: Challenge: Use TWO different directional terms in ONE sentence to describe a body relationship.
Example format: 'Structure A is [term 1] to Structure B, and [term 2] to Structure C.'
Try: Use the navel, the chin, and the spine as your three structures.
Share your sentence with the class — we'll vote on whether it is accurate.
Remember: ALL statements assume anatomical position.
slides.youTry: Sample answer: 'The navel is inferior to the chin and anterior to the spine.'

slides.heading: This Week's Plan
bullets: TODAY: Directional terms — applying all 5 pairs to real body structures.
Day 2: Body planes and sections (sagittal, frontal, transverse) — how we 'slice' the body.
Day 3: Body cavities and their contents — where major organs live.
Day 4: Review + application — putting planes, cavities, and directional terms together.
Quiz: End of the week — you will describe organ locations using directional terms AND planes.

procedureExamples.prompt: Is the liver superior or inferior to the diaphragm?
steps: Step 1: Identify the two structures — liver and diaphragm.
Step 2: We are comparing along the head-to-foot axis, so we use superior/inferior.
Step 3: The diaphragm sits higher in the body (closer to the head) than the liver.
Step 4: Therefore, the liver is INFERIOR to the diaphragm.
procedureExamples.answer: The liver is inferior to the diaphragm.

procedureExamples.prompt: Is the fibula (the thin bone on the outer side of the lower leg) medial or lateral to the tibia (the shin bone) in anatomical position? Explain your reasoning.
steps: Step 1: Identify structures — radius (thumb side) and ulna (pinky side) of the forearm.
Step 2: In anatomical position, palms face forward, so the thumb faces outward — away from the body midline.
Step 3: The radius is on the thumb side → farther from the body midline → LATERAL.
Step 4: The radius is lateral to the ulna (and the ulna is medial to the radius).
procedureExamples.answer: The radius is lateral to the ulna.

procedureExamples.prompt: A surgeon describes two tumors in the abdomen: one located just beneath the skin layer and one embedded deep within the abdominal muscle. Use superficial and deep to describe where each tumor is relative to the other.
steps: Step 1: Structures — skin surface and muscle layer.
Step 2: Use the superficial/deep axis — this describes distance from the body's outer surface.
Step 3: Skin is closer to the surface → superficial; muscle is farther from the surface → deep.
Step 4: The skin laceration is SUPERFICIAL to the muscle; the muscle is DEEP to the skin.
procedureExamples.answer: The skin wound is superficial to the muscle; the muscle is deep to the skin.

worksheet.title: Directional Terms Practice
worksheet.instructions: Use your guided notes and the word bank to complete all sections. Write in complete sentences where indicated. All descriptions assume the body is in anatomical position.

sections.type: Section 1 — Choose the Correct Directional Term
sections.workedExample:
**Example:** Is the forehead superior or inferior to the chin?
- Step 1: Structures = forehead and chin.
- Step 2: Axis = head-to-foot → use superior/inferior.
- Step 3: Forehead is closer to the top of the head.
- **Answer: The forehead is SUPERIOR to the chin.**
