formulas.name: Homeostasis
formulas.formula: The body's ability to maintain a stable internal environment despite outside changes

formulas.name: Negative feedback
formulas.formula: A response that REVERSES the original stimulus to restore balance

formulas.name: Anatomical position
formulas.formula: Standing, arms at sides, palms forward — the universal reference for all directional terms

formulas.name: Superior / Inferior
formulas.formula: Superior = toward the head; Inferior = toward the feet

formulas.name: Medial / Lateral
formulas.formula: Medial = toward the midline; Lateral = away from the midline

vocab.def: A {{change in the internal or external environment|3cm}} that is detected by the body and triggers a response.
The structure (usually the {{hypothalamus or brain|3cm}}) that receives information from receptors and directs the body's response.
The organ or tissue that {{carries out the response|3cm}} directed by the control center — for example, sweat glands or muscles.

examples.label: Concept 1 — Levels of Organization in a Patient Scenario
examples.prompt: A patient tears the cartilage in her knee. At what level of organization is the injury, and what HIGHER level is immediately disrupted?
steps: Identify the injured structure: cartilage is a type of {{connective tissue|2.5cm}} — so the injury is at the TISSUE level.
The knee joint is formed by multiple tissues working together, making it an {{organ|1.5cm}}.
When the organ cannot function normally, the musculoskeletal {{organ system|2cm}} is disrupted.
Conclusion: injury starts at the tissue level and disrupts the {{organ system|2cm}} level.
examples.answer: Tissue level injured; organ system level disrupted (musculoskeletal system).

examples.label: Concept 2 — Applying Directional Terms
examples.prompt: A paramedic notes a laceration that is 'superior and medial to the right knee.' Where exactly is that cut?
steps: Superior means {{above / toward the head|2.5cm}} — so the cut is above the knee.
Medial means {{toward the midline of the body|3cm}} — so the cut is on the inner side.
Combined: the laceration is on the {{upper, inner|2cm}} portion of the right leg, near the thigh.
examples.answer: Upper inner right leg / lower medial thigh, above the knee joint.

examples.label: Concept 3 — Tracing a Feedback Loop
examples.prompt: A runner's blood glucose drops below normal. Identify the stimulus, control center, effector, and type of feedback.
steps: Stimulus: {{blood glucose falls below normal range|3.5cm}} (hypoglycemia).
Control center: the {{pancreas (alpha cells) / liver|3cm}} detects the drop and releases glucagon.
Effector: the {{liver|1.5cm}} breaks down glycogen and releases glucose into the blood.
This is {{negative|1.5cm}} feedback because the response (glucose rises) reverses the original stimulus.
examples.answer: Negative feedback: low glucose → pancreas → liver releases glucose → blood glucose rises back to normal.

youTry.prompt: Name the body cavity that contains the stomach and liver.
youTry.answer: Thoracic cavity (specifically the pericardial cavity for the heart and pleural cavities for the lungs).

youTry.prompt: A patient has a bruise on the anterior surface of the left forearm, closer to the wrist than the elbow. Use TWO directional terms to describe the bruise's location relative to the elbow.
youTry.answer: The bruise is DISTAL (farther from the trunk / closer to the wrist) and ANTERIOR (on the front surface) relative to the elbow.

guidedNotes.summary: The body maintains {{homeostasis|2.5cm}} through feedback loops: a stimulus is detected by a {{receptor|2cm}}, processed by a control center, and corrected by an {{effector|2cm}} — directional terms and knowledge of body levels help clinicians describe exactly WHERE and WHAT is disrupted.

Fri.notesExit: Describe in 1-2 sentences how the SAME heat-stroke scenario involves at least TWO different levels of organization AND a negative feedback loop — name the stimulus, control center, and one effector.

vocab.definition: Any change detected by the body that triggers a response (e.g., rising body temperature).
The structure that detects a stimulus and sends a signal to the control center.
The structure (commonly the hypothalamus) that evaluates the signal and directs a corrective response.
The organ or tissue that carries out the control center's instructions to restore homeostasis.
A feedback mechanism in which the response REDUCES or reverses the original stimulus, restoring balance.
The standard reference posture: standing erect, arms at sides, palms facing forward.

presentation.title: Week Synthesis: Applying A&P Concepts to a Real Case

slides.heading: The Scenario: El Paso August, Football Practice
bullets: Marcus, 19, collapses during two-a-day practice; skin is hot and dry; he's confused.
His core temperature reads 40.5 °C — more than 3° above the homeostatic set point of 37 °C.
His sweating has STOPPED — the effector system has failed.
Question: Which body SYSTEMS are failing, and at what LEVEL of organization is the damage happening?
Today's goal: use every concept from this week to analyze this ONE real situation.

slides.heading: The Four Tools You Bring to This Case
bullets: 1 — LEVELS OF ORGANIZATION: chemical → cellular → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
2 — DIRECTIONAL TERMS: superior/inferior, anterior/posterior, medial/lateral, proximal/distal
3 — BODY REGIONS & CAVITIES: cranial, thoracic, abdominal, pelvic — plus surface regions (brachial, femoral, etc.)
4 — HOMEOSTASIS & FEEDBACK LOOPS: stimulus → receptor → control center → effector → response
Word bank on your worksheet has every term you need — use it!

slides.heading: Worked Example — Tracing Marcus's Feedback Loop
bullets: STIMULUS: core body temperature rises above 37 °C (detected by thermoreceptors in the skin and blood).
CONTROL CENTER: hypothalamus receives the signal and sends commands via the nervous system.
EFFECTOR: sweat glands should produce sweat → evaporation cools the skin → temperature drops.
In heat stroke, the sweat glands FAIL — the feedback loop is BROKEN and temperature keeps climbing.
Level of organization: sweat glands = organs; their failure disrupts the integumentary organ system → whole organism at risk.
slides.example:
Step 1 — Identify stimulus: blood pressure drops below normal set point.
Step 2 — Receptor: baroreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid sinus detect the drop.
Step 3 — Control center: medulla oblongata integrates the signal.
Step 4 — Effector: heart increases rate and force; blood vessels constrict.
Step 5 — Outcome: blood pressure rises back toward set point → negative feedback loop maintained.

slides.heading: The Feedback Loop — Refer to This While You Work
bullets: Follow the arrows: Stimulus → Receptor → Control Center → Effector → Response
In NEGATIVE feedback the response REVERSES the stimulus (temperature goes back down).
In Marcus's case the effector (sweat glands) failed — locate where the loop BROKE.
Your worksheet asks you to draw and label your OWN version of this loop for his scenario.
slides.graphCaption: Negative feedback loop — body temperature example. The response reverses the original stimulus.

slides.heading: We-Do: Apply Directional Terms to Marcus
bullets: Paramedics note two injuries from the fall: (A) a cut on the front of his left shin, and (B) a bruise on the outer upper arm.
For injury A: Is the shin ANTERIOR or POSTERIOR? Is it SUPERIOR or INFERIOR to the knee?
For injury B: Is the outer upper arm MEDIAL or LATERAL to the body's midline? Is it PROXIMAL or DISTAL to the shoulder?
Discuss with a partner — be ready to share your directional term choices.
slides.youTry: Injury A: posterior surface, superior to the elbow. Injury B: medial, proximal to the left knee. For each injury, identify the two directional terms used and describe exactly where the injury is located.

procedureExamples.prompt: Using the case scenario: Elena, a cyclist, fractures her femur (thigh bone). (a) What level of organization is a bone such as the femur? (b) What organ SYSTEM is disrupted by this fracture? (c) What body CAVITY is immediately superior to the region where the femur is found?
steps: Step 1 — Identify the level: kidneys are discrete structures made of multiple tissue types → ORGAN level.
Step 2 — Identify the system: the kidneys are part of the URINARY (renal) organ system.
Step 3 — Identify the cavity: the kidneys sit in the RETROPERITONEAL space of the ABDOMINAL cavity (posterior to the peritoneum).
Step 4 — State the homeostasis impact: kidney failure means blood waste levels rise, fluid balance fails — homeostasis of the internal environment is severely disrupted.
procedureExamples.answer: (a) Organ level; (b) Urinary system; (c) Abdominal cavity (retroperitoneal).

procedureExamples.prompt: A medic describes a wound as being 'on the anterior, medial surface of the right thigh, proximal to the knee.' Point to that location on your own body and explain what each term means.
steps: Step 1 — Anterior: front surface of the body → front of the thigh.
Step 2 — Medial: toward the body's midline → inner side of the thigh.
Step 3 — Proximal to the knee: closer to the trunk / upper portion of the thigh.
Step 4 — Combined location: upper-inner FRONT of the right thigh.
procedureExamples.answer: Upper inner front surface of the right thigh.

worksheet.title: Case Study Synthesis Worksheet — Marcus & the Heat Stroke
worksheet.instructions:
Read the scenario below, then answer each section using your word bank and guided notes. Every answer should reference details from the scenario.

**SCENARIO:** Marcus (age 19) collapses during August football practice in El Paso. His skin is hot and dry; he is confused; his core temperature is 40.5 °C. Paramedics arrive and note: (1) a superficial laceration on the anterior surface of his left shin, inferior to the knee; (2) a bruise on the lateral surface of his right upper arm, proximal to the elbow; (3) his sweating has completely stopped. He is transported to the hospital where doctors find early kidney stress.

**Word Bank:** stimulus · receptor · control center · effector · negative feedback · homeostasis · superior · inferior · anterior · posterior · medial · lateral · proximal · distal · thoracic cavity · abdominal cavity · pelvic cavity · cranial cavity · organ · organ system · tissue · cell

sections.workedExample:
**Example:** The paramedic says Marcus's *skin* is hot and dry. The skin is composed of epithelial tissue, connective tissue, nerves, and blood vessels — multiple tissue types working together. Therefore, skin is at the **organ** level of organization, and it belongs to the **integumentary organ system**.

*Step 1: Identify the structure → Step 2: Ask 'is it one type of molecule, one cell, one tissue type, or multiple tissues?' → Step 3: Name the level and the organ system it belongs to.*
sections.directions: Directions: For each structure named in the scenario, identify its level of organization AND the organ system it belongs to.
problems: 1. Marcus's **kidneys** are stressed. (a) What level of organization are the kidneys? (b) What organ system do they belong to?
2. The heat is damaging individual **muscle cells** in Marcus's legs. What level of organization is a single muscle cell?
3. The group of **muscle fibers (muscle tissue)** in Marcus's thigh is struggling to contract. What level of organization is muscle tissue?

🌶 4. Marcus's condition is deteriorating at the level of the whole **organism**. Explain why a disruption at the ORGAN level (kidneys) can eventually threaten the organism level — use the levels of organization hierarchy in your answer.

sections.workedExample:
**Example:** 'Marcus has a bruise on the *posterior* surface of his right heel, *distal* to the ankle.'

*Step 1:* Posterior = back surface of the body. *Step 2:* Distal = farther from the trunk (in the lower limb, farther from the hip). *Step 3:* Location = back of the heel, below and away from the ankle joint. ✓
sections.directions: Directions: Use the word bank directional terms to answer each question about Marcus's injuries. Write the term AND a one-sentence explanation.
problems: 5. The laceration is on the **front** of Marcus's left shin. Which directional term describes this surface — anterior or posterior?
6. The laceration is **below** the knee. Which directional term applies — superior or inferior?
7. The bruise on Marcus's right upper arm is on the **outer** side (away from the midline). Which term applies — medial or lateral?
8. The upper arm bruise is **closer to the shoulder** than to the elbow. Which term describes this position relative to the shoulder — proximal or distal?
9. Marcus's heart is located **closer to the midline** than his lungs. Use the correct directional term to describe the heart's position relative to the lungs.

🌶 10. A doctor notes that Marcus's liver is **inferior to the diaphragm** and **anterior to the right kidney**. Write a complete sentence using BOTH directional terms to describe the liver's position relative to EACH of the two structures.

sections.workedExample:
**Example:** The heart is located in the **thoracic cavity**, specifically within the mediastinum (the central region between the two lungs). The thoracic cavity is superior to the abdominal cavity and is separated from it by the **diaphragm**.

*Step 1: Name the organ → Step 2: Name its cavity → Step 3: Note what borders or separates that cavity from adjacent ones.*
sections.directions: Directions: Use the scenario and your notes to identify the correct body cavity or region for each item.
problems: 11. Marcus's **kidneys** are found in this cavity: _______________
12. The **heart and lungs** that are working hard to compensate for his heat stroke are located in the _______________ cavity.
13. The **urinary bladder** (part of the urinary system also stressed by heat stroke) is located in the _______________ cavity.
14. Name the structure (a single muscle/membrane) that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity: _______________

sections.workedExample:
**Example — Tracing a Full Feedback Loop:** A healthy person exercises; blood CO₂ rises.

- **Stimulus:** CO₂ level rises above normal.
- **Receptor:** chemoreceptors in the brainstem detect the increase.
- **Control center:** brainstem respiratory centers increase breathing rate.
- **Effector:** diaphragm and intercostal muscles contract faster → more CO₂ exhaled.
- **Response:** CO₂ returns to normal level.
- **Type:** Negative feedback — the response (lower CO₂) reverses the stimulus (high CO₂).

*Step 1: Identify stimulus → Step 2: Receptor → Step 3: Control center → Step 4: Effector → Step 5: Response → Step 6: Name the feedback type.*
sections.directions: Directions: Use Marcus's heat-stroke scenario to complete the feedback loop analysis below. Fill in each component and answer the short questions.
problems: 15. **Stimulus:** What is the specific change in Marcus's body that triggered the temperature-regulation feedback loop? Write one complete sentence.
16. **Receptor:** What type of receptor detects changes in body temperature?
17. **Control center:** Name the brain structure that normally serves as the control center for body temperature.
18. **Effector:** In a healthy person, what organ/structure is the primary effector for cooling the body? What does it do?
19. **Broken loop:** Marcus's sweating stopped (effector failure). Explain in ONE sentence why this makes heat stroke so dangerous — use the word 'homeostasis' in your answer.

🌶 20. If paramedics apply **ice packs to Marcus's neck, armpits, and groin** to rapidly cool him, are they acting as an artificial RECEPTOR, CONTROL CENTER, or EFFECTOR in the feedback loop? Justify your choice in 2 sentences.

procedure: Read the scenario carefully and underline key anatomical details before answering.
Use the Word Bank — every term you need is listed there.
For feedback loops: always identify all 4 components (stimulus → receptor → control center → effector) AND name the feedback type.
Use anatomical position as your reference whenever applying directional terms.
optionalExtra: CHALLENGE A: Design your OWN brief clinical scenario (3-4 sentences) that requires a classmate to use (1) at least two directional terms, (2) one body cavity, and (3) one complete feedback loop. Then provide a full answer key for your scenario.

CHALLENGE B: Marcus's condition is a failure of NEGATIVE feedback. Describe what a POSITIVE feedback loop looks like using the example of blood clotting after a cut — name the stimulus, how the response amplifies rather than reverses it, and how the loop eventually ends.

extension.title: Challenge: Design-a-Disruption
extension.prompt: Choose ONE body system (cardiovascular, respiratory, or nervous). Write a 4-sentence mini case study describing a patient whose homeostasis is disrupted in that system. Your case must (a) name the stimulus, (b) identify at least two levels of organization affected, (c) use three directional terms to describe where symptoms appear, and (d) explain whether the body's feedback response is negative feedback working correctly, or a broken/failed feedback loop — and why it matters for survival.
extension.why: Extends all four week skills simultaneously in a generative (design-your-own) format — requires deeper integration than completing a pre-written scenario.

exitTicket: Name the FOUR components of a feedback loop and give a one-word example of a stimulus that would trigger a temperature-regulation response in the human body.
A patient has pain in the inferior, medial surface of the right thigh — describe in plain language exactly where on the body that is, and name the body cavity closest to that region.

answerKey.procedure: Identify structure → determine complexity (single molecule/cell/one tissue type/multiple tissues) → match to the hierarchy level → name the associated organ system.
answers: 1. (a) Organ level — the kidney is a discrete structure composed of multiple tissue types (epithelial, connective, nervous, vascular) working together. (b) Urinary (renal) organ system.
2. Cell level — a single muscle cell (muscle fiber) is one structural unit of life, the fundamental level above the chemical/molecular level.
3. Tissue level — muscle tissue is a group of similar cells (muscle fibers) working together to perform contraction; it is above the cellular level but below the organ level.

🌶 4. The levels of organization are hierarchical — disruption at a lower level cascades upward. Kidney failure (organ level) means the body cannot filter waste or regulate fluid balance. These functions are essential for every organ system (cardiovascular, nervous, etc.). When multiple organ systems fail, the whole organism cannot maintain homeostasis and survival is threatened. Organ-level failure thus endangers organism-level survival because each higher level depends on the proper functioning of all lower levels.

answerKey.procedure: Recall anatomical position (standing, palms forward) as the universal reference → apply the correct term from each pair based on the relationship described.
answers: 5. Anterior — the front surface of the body in anatomical position. The shin laceration is on the anterior (front-facing) surface of the left lower leg.
6. Inferior — inferior means toward the feet / below. The laceration is below (inferior to) the knee joint.
7. Lateral — lateral means away from the body's midline. The outer side of the arm is farther from the midline, so it is the lateral surface.
8. Proximal — in the limbs, proximal means closer to the point of attachment to the trunk (the shoulder). The upper arm bruise is proximal relative to the elbow (the elbow would be distal).
9. Medial — the heart is closer to the body's midline than the lungs. Therefore the heart is medial to the lungs (and the lungs are lateral to the heart).

🌶 10. Example complete sentence: 'The liver is inferior to the diaphragm and anterior to the right kidney.' — inferior: the liver sits below the diaphragm (toward the feet); anterior: the liver is in front of the right kidney when viewed in anatomical position.

answerKey.procedure: Associate each major organ with its body cavity using the standard cavity map: cranial (brain), thoracic (heart/lungs), abdominal (digestive organs, kidneys), pelvic (bladder, reproductive organs).
answers: 11. Abdominal cavity (retroperitoneal region) — the kidneys lie posterior to the peritoneum within the abdominal cavity.
12. Thoracic cavity — the heart and lungs are enclosed within the thoracic cavity, protected by the rib cage and sternum.
13. Pelvic cavity — the urinary bladder is located in the inferior portion of the ventral body cavity, within the pelvic cavity.
14. The diaphragm — a dome-shaped skeletal muscle that forms the floor of the thoracic cavity and the roof of the abdominal cavity, separating the two.

answerKey.procedure: For every feedback loop: identify stimulus → receptor → control center → effector → describe the response → determine whether it reverses (negative) or amplifies (positive) the stimulus.
answers: 15. Stimulus: Marcus's core body temperature rose significantly above the normal set point of 37 °C (reaching 40.5 °C) during intense exercise in extreme heat, triggering the thermoregulatory feedback loop.
16. Thermoreceptors (temperature receptors) — peripheral thermoreceptors in the skin and central thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the temperature increase.
17. The hypothalamus — located in the brain, it is the primary control center for thermoregulation and integrates temperature signals to direct the body's cooling responses.
18. Sweat glands (part of the integumentary system) — they produce sweat onto the skin surface; as sweat evaporates, it carries heat away from the body, lowering core temperature.

19. Because the sweat glands (the effector) have failed, the body can no longer produce the cooling response needed to reverse the rising temperature, so homeostasis cannot be restored and core temperature continues to climb to life-threatening levels.

🌶 20. The paramedics are acting as an artificial EFFECTOR. In the feedback loop, the effector is the structure that performs the corrective action directed by the control center. By applying ice packs, the paramedics are physically carrying out the cooling response (lowering skin and blood temperature) that Marcus's own sweat glands (the normal effector) can no longer perform — they are substituting for the failed effector, not detecting the stimulus (receptor) or processing information (control center).

answerKey.procedure: Open-ended synthesis — evaluate for correct use of all required concepts, internal consistency, and accuracy.
answers: CHALLENGE A: Student-created scenario — award full credit if it includes: (1) two correctly used and defined directional terms, (2) one correctly named body cavity with an organ inside it, and (3) a complete four-part feedback loop (stimulus, receptor, control center, effector) with the feedback type named. Deduct partial credit for missing components.

CHALLENGE B: Blood clotting (positive feedback) — Stimulus: a blood vessel is cut and platelets contact exposed collagen. Response: platelets release chemicals that recruit MORE platelets and clotting factors — the response amplifies the original signal rather than reversing it (positive feedback). The loop ends (is shut off) when the clot fully seals the vessel and no more exposed collagen is available, removing the stimulus. Key distinction from negative feedback: the response intensifies until a defined endpoint is reached, then stops.
